units.title: Period 1: 1491–1607
units.blurb: Maize, the Pueblo and Iroquois, Columbus, the Columbian Exchange, encomienda, the Pueblo Revolt and the first enslaved Africans. Questions compare Native societies by environment and trace the effects of contact.
keys: Maize farming spread north from Mexico and let peoples such as the Pueblo build permanent, irrigated, socially stratified towns.
Native societies fit their environments, from Pueblo irrigation farmers to mobile Plains bison hunters and salmon-rich Chinook villages.
Cahokia's mounds and the Iroquois Confederacy prove North America held cities and complex governments long before 1492.
God, gold and glory, backed by the caravel, compass and astrolabe, carried Columbus to the Caribbean for Spain in 1492.
The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals and disease both ways and collapsed Native populations through epidemic disease.
Spain ruled through encomienda labor, the casta hierarchy and missions, a system Las Casas denounced at Valladolid in 1550.
As Native labor collapsed, Spain and Portugal imported enslaved Africans on the sugar plantation model built at Madeira and Sao Tome.
Native peoples resisted as well as adapted, most successfully in the 1680 Pueblo Revolt that expelled Spain from New Mexico.

topics.t: Native American societies before European contact
Columbian Exchange, Spanish exploration, and conquest
Labor, slavery, and caste in the Spanish colonial system
Cultural interactions between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

excl.s: Optional Sources pages offer examples of sources appropriate for a college-level course. None of the AP Exam questions require students to have studied these specific sources.

units.check: Progress check · 15 multiple choice · 2 short answer (primary source (partial), primary source (partial)) · 1 free response (long essay (partial))

frq.title: SAQ 1 · Who conquered Mexico? (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"For five centuries the fall of Tenochtitlan has been told as the triumph of a few hundred Spaniards over an empire of millions. That story mistakes the flag for the army. The warriors who besieged the Mexica capital in 1521 were overwhelmingly Tlaxcalans, Texcocans, and other Native peoples who saw in the strangers a chance to end the tribute and captive-taking the Triple Alliance imposed on them. Smallpox, arriving in 1520, did the rest, killing the Mexica ruler Cuitlahuac and thousands of defenders. The conquest of Mexico was, in large part, a Mesoamerican war whose winners soon discovered they had exchanged one overlord for another."

Elena Ruiz-Hartley, historian, The Allied Conquest, 2019. (The historian and the book are fictional, written for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the Spanish conquest of the Aztec (Mexica) Empire.
parts.a: The historian argues that the fall of Tenochtitlan was mainly the work of Native peoples and disease rather than of Spanish power: Tlaxcalans, Texcocans and other subject peoples, resentful of Mexica tribute and captive-taking, made up most of the besieging army, and the smallpox epidemic of 1520 killed the ruler Cuitlahuac and many defenders, so the Spaniards were a small part of the victory.
parts.n: Quoting the excerpt, or writing 'the historian talks about the conquest', earns nothing; describe the claim (allies and disease, not Spanish strength, won) in your own words.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1492 to 1607, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, supports the historian's argument.
parts.a: Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire (1532-1533) supports it. Fewer than 200 Spaniards succeeded because smallpox had already killed the Inca ruler Huayna Capac and set off a civil war between his sons Atahualpa and Huascar, so Andean divisions and disease, not Spanish numbers, decided the outcome, the same pattern the historian finds in Mexico. (Also accepted: Malintzin's translation making the Tlaxcalan alliance possible; Spain's later reliance on Tlaxcalan colonists to end the Chichimeca War.)
parts.n: Reusing the excerpt's own evidence (the Tlaxcalans, the 1520 epidemic) earns nothing; the development must be new and tied to the argument.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1492 to 1607 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: Tlaxcala had fought the Mexica for decades without taking Tenochtitlan, so the new element in 1519-1521 was Spanish: Cortes organized the coalition, and Spaniards built thirteen brigantines that cut the island city off by water during the 1521 siege. The Spanish role was therefore decisive even if Spaniards were few. (Also accepted: the conquest of the Caribbean islands, where Spaniards subdued the Taino without large Native allied armies.)
parts.n: Simply disagreeing ('the Spanish did win') earns nothing; the point needs a specific development and an explanation of how it limits the historian's claim.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · A town petitions the king (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"To our lord the King: We, the governors and nobles of this town, kiss your royal hands. When the Marques [Cortes] came, we received him in peace, gave him food and warriors, and our men died in the war against Mexico in your service. Now the encomendero to whom we have been given demands tribute in cloth, maize, and gold beyond what our fathers paid to Moctezuma, and he sends our people to the mines, where many die. Our fields go unplanted and our children go hungry. We ask that you command that we pay only what is just, as your laws declare, and that our town be placed under your royal crown."

Described period document: a petition from the council of an Indigenous town in central Mexico to the king of Spain, 1560. It was composed for this exercise on the model of the petitions, written in Nahuatl or Spanish, that Indigenous town councils sent to the Spanish crown in the mid-1500s.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which the petition was written.
parts.a: By 1560 Spain ruled central Mexico, which it had conquered in 1519-1521 with the help of Native allies, and had granted Native towns in encomienda to Spanish colonists who collected tribute and labor for mines and farms. Epidemics were shrinking Native populations, so the same demands fell on fewer people, and the New Laws of 1542 had given the crown a legal basis to limit encomenderos, which Native towns invoked in petitions like this one.
parts.n: Summarizing the document ('they are complaining about tribute') describes its content, not its historical situation; the point needs the conquest, the encomienda and the crown's reforms around it.

parts.q: Explain how the purpose or the audience of the petition shaped its content.
parts.a: Written to persuade the king to relieve the town, the petition stresses the town's loyalty and its warriors' service in the conquest, contrasts the encomendero's excessive demands with the lighter tribute paid under Moctezuma, and appeals to the king's own laws. The leaders present themselves as faithful vassals wronged by a subordinate, the framing most likely to move a monarch who was already trying to rein in encomenderos.
parts.n: Identifying the audience ('it is written to the king') without explaining how that audience shaped what the town chose to say earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain ONE way the Spanish colonial labor system changed in the period 1492 to 1607.
parts.a: Spain shifted from private encomienda grants toward crown-controlled labor drafts and enslaved African labor. After the Caribbean population collapsed and the New Laws of 1542 barred new encomiendas and the enslavement of Native people, the crown channeled Native labor through state drafts such as the repartimiento in New Spain and the Potosi mita (1573), while planters and mine owners imported growing numbers of enslaved Africans.
parts.n: Saying labor 'got worse' or 'changed' without naming the specific shift and why it happened earns nothing.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · The population of central Mexico, 1518-1605 (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the graph described below.

Described line graph, titled 'Estimated Native Population of Central Mexico, 1518-1605'. Horizontal axis: year, 1518 to 1605. Vertical axis: population in millions, 0 to 30. Seven points joined by a line:
Year · Estimated population (millions)
1518 · 25.2
1532 · 16.8
1548 · 6.3
1568 · 2.65
1580 · 1.9
1595 · 1.375
1605 · 1.075
The line drops steeply from 1518 to 1548, then falls more slowly and flattens just above 1 million after 1595.

Source: data from estimates published by the historians Sherburne F. Cook and Woodrow Borah (1960s-1970s); graph described for this exercise.

parts.q: Identify ONE pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: The Native population of central Mexico fell by roughly 96 percent, from about 25.2 million in 1518 to about 1.1 million in 1605, and the fall was steepest in the first three decades (to 6.3 million by 1548) before slowing after 1568.
parts.n: 'The population went down' is too vague; state the direction with the scale or the timing the graph shows.

parts.q: Explain ONE cause of the pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: Epidemics of diseases from Europe and Africa, to which Native peoples had no acquired immunity, were the main cause: smallpox struck during the conquest in 1520, and later great epidemics, including the cocoliztli outbreaks of 1545-1548 and the late 1570s, line up with the graph's steepest drops. Forced labor, tribute and famine under the encomienda weakened survivors and made each outbreak deadlier.
parts.n: 'Disease' with no mechanism or example earns little; the point needs the lack of immunity or a named epidemic linked to the decline. What cocoliztli was is still debated.

parts.q: Explain ONE effect of the pattern shown in the graph on Spanish colonial society in the period 1519 to 1607.
parts.a: The collapse shrank the tribute and labor base on which the encomienda depended, so the crown restricted encomiendas (New Laws, 1542), organized the survivors' labor through state drafts (the repartimiento), and forcibly resettled scattered survivors into compact towns (congregaciones, around 1600), while colonists turned increasingly to enslaved Africans for labor.
parts.n: An effect asserted without a link to the population loss ('Spain needed workers') earns nothing; connect the decline to a specific Spanish response.

frq.title: DBQ · Religion and the European conquest of the Americas, 1492-1607
frq.stem:
Practice. The exam draws its DBQ from 1754 to 1980, so none comes from Period 1; this one practises the same seven-point skills on Period 1 content.

Evaluate the extent to which religious motives shaped European conquest and colonization in the Americas from 1492 to 1607.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; the wording is not a direct quotation.

Document 1
Source: Christopher Columbus, letter announcing his first voyage, addressed to Luis de Santangel, a financial official of the Spanish crown, 1493.
"The islands are fertile beyond description, with fine harbors, many spices, and great mines of gold. The people go unarmed, are timid, and give whatever they have for trifles. They know no sect or idolatry, and I believe they would readily become Christians. Their Highnesses may have as much gold as they need, spices and cotton, and slaves, as many as they order, taken from the idolaters."

Document 2
Source: The Requerimiento, a statement drafted for the Spanish crown by the jurist Juan Lopez de Palacios Rubios in 1513, to be read aloud by Spanish commanders to Native peoples before fighting began.
"We ask that you acknowledge the Church as ruler of the whole world, and the pope, and in his name the king and queen of Spain, and that you allow the faith to be preached to you. If you do so, we will receive you with love. If you do not, or maliciously delay, with the help of God we shall make war on you, enslave you, your wives, and your children, and take your goods; and the deaths and losses that follow will be your fault, not ours."

Document 3
Source: Hernan Cortes, second letter to Emperor Charles V, 1520, reporting on his entry into Tenochtitlan.
"The city is as large as Seville or Cordoba. It has a square where more than sixty thousand people come each day to buy and sell every kind of goods: gold, silver, precious stones, and feathers. In the principal temple I had the idols thrown down the steps and the chapels cleansed of the blood of sacrifices, and I set up images of Our Lady and the saints there, which grieved Moctezuma and his people."

Document 4
Source: Bartolome de las Casas, Dominican friar and former encomendero, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 for Emperor Charles V and printed in 1552.
"The reason the Christians have killed and destroyed such an infinite number of souls is solely that they have made gold their ultimate aim, seeking to grow rich in a very short time. They have cared no more for the souls of these peoples, the humblest and most peaceful in the world, than for beasts, and have killed them before they could hear of the faith."

Document 5
Source: Juan Gines de Sepulveda, Spanish scholar and royal chronicler, Democrates Alter, a dialogue written about 1544 defending the justice of war against Native peoples; he argued the same case at Valladolid in 1550.
"Compare the prudence and virtue of the Spaniards with these barbarians, who are as inferior to the Spaniards as children are to adults. They worship idols and offer human sacrifice. It is therefore just that they be ruled by the Spaniards, and war to subject them is lawful, for it ends their crimes against nature and opens the way for the preaching of the Christian religion."

Document 6
Source: Account of the conquest by Nahua elders, recorded in Nahuatl in the Florentine Codex, compiled from the 1550s to about 1577 under the direction of the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun.
"When the Spaniards were given the gold banners and necklaces, they rejoiced. They seized the gold like monkeys; it satisfied and gladdened their hearts. They hungered for it like pigs. Later they went into Moctezuma's treasure house and took everything, the gold and the jewels, as if it were their own."

Document 7
Source: Richard Hakluyt, English clergyman and geographer, Discourse of Western Planting, written in 1584 for Queen Elizabeth I to urge support for English colonies in North America.
"This western voyage will greatly enlarge the gospel of Christ, a duty that falls chiefly on the princes of the reformed religion, since the Spaniards have converted the people only in name and with cruelty. Planting there will also supply the commodities we now buy from our enemies, give a market for our woolen cloth, set our idle poor to work, and give us a base from which to trouble the King of Spain and cut off his treasure."

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: religion shaped conquest mainly as a justification and partner of the pursuit of wealth: Spain's crown made conversion the legal key to war, land and labor (Docs 2, 5), conquerors pursued gold under a religious banner (Docs 1, 3, 4, 6), and by the 1580s English promoters fused Protestant mission with commerce and rivalry (Doc 7).
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('religion shaped colonization to some extent'), a claim with no line of reasoning, or a thesis split between introduction and conclusion.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, beyond a phrase: e.g., the Reconquista's crusading tradition, completed at Granada in 1492, which fused conquest, reward and conversion; or the Protestant Reformation after 1517, which split Europe and turned imperial rivalry into religious rivalry.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'during the Age of Exploration' or 'Europeans wanted God, gold, and glory'; context unconnected to the prompt.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument (e.g., Doc 2's demand to accept the Church on pain of war and slavery; Doc 3's destruction of idols beside the gold of the market; Docs 4 and 6 on greed for gold; Doc 7's mix of Protestant, commercial and anti-Spanish aims). 1 point: accurately describes the content of three documents that address the topic.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing their content; describing fewer than three; misreading a document (e.g., treating Doc 4 as a defense of conquest).

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific, described piece of evidence not in the documents and different from the context, e.g.: the encomienda, which granted Native labor on condition that the holder Christianize the workers; Potosi silver (from 1545) and the mita; Franciscan missions in Florida and New Mexico (from 1598); the New Laws of 1542.
rows.loses: A name dropped without description ('the encomienda'), evidence already in a document, or the same evidence used for contextualization.

rows.earns: For two documents, explains how or why point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience is relevant to the argument, e.g.: Doc 1's purpose, winning a larger second voyage, explains why converts are paired with gold and slaves; Doc 5 was written to defend conquest by a scholar who never went to the Americas; Doc 6 records Nahua memory decades later under a Franciscan's direction, which may sharpen its criticism of lay Spaniards' greed; Doc 7's audience, the queen and investors, explains the Protestant appeal tied to profit.
rows.loses: Identifying the author or date ('Doc 4 was written by Las Casas in 1542') without explaining why that matters to the argument.

rows.earns: A complex understanding woven into the argument, e.g.: explains that religious and economic motives reinforced each other (the Requerimiento made refusing conversion the legal ground for seizing land and labor); distinguishes Spanish Catholic and English Protestant uses of religion; or uses Docs 4-6 to show Europeans themselves disputing whether faith justified conquest.
rows.loses: A single sentence noting 'there were many motives', or a counterargument that is stated but not explained or tied to the thesis.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Religious motives shaped European conquest mainly as a justification for, and partner of, the pursuit of wealth: Spain made conversion the legal key that unlocked war, land and Native labor, conquerors sought gold under a Christian banner, and English promoters by the 1580s fused Protestant mission with commerce and rivalry with Spain.
parts.n: A thesis that says only 'religion and wealth both mattered' does not establish a line of reasoning; say how the two were related.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Open with the Reconquista: seven centuries of Christian war against Muslim Iberia ended at Granada in January 1492, leaving Spain's monarchs with a crusading ideal and a practice of rewarding conquerors with land and the labor of the defeated. Add that Portugal's African voyages and the search for Asian trade made wealth a parallel motive, and that after 1517 the Reformation made religion a line of rivalry among European states.
parts.n: Two or three sentences that describe developments and connect them to the prompt; a single phrase earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan which documents support which part of the argument.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, religion as legal justification: Doc 2 (accept the Church or face war and slavery), Doc 5 (idolatry and sacrifice make war just), Doc 3 (idols thrown down and replaced). Paragraph 2, wealth as the driving motive: Doc 1 (gold and slaves promised beside converts), Doc 4 (gold the 'ultimate aim'), Doc 6 (Nahua memory of Spaniards seizing gold 'like monkeys'), Doc 3 (the market's gold and silver). Paragraph 3, a Protestant variation: Doc 7 (gospel, cloth markets, idle poor, attacks on Spain). Using six or seven documents also supports complexity.
parts.n: Describe each document's content in your own words and tie it to the claim; a list of document numbers earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece and say where it goes.
parts.a: In paragraph 1: the encomienda, which gave a colonist the tribute and labor of a Native district on condition that he protect and Christianize its people, shows religion written into the labor system that produced wealth. Alternative for paragraph 2: Potosi silver (opened 1545), worked by drafted Native laborers under the mita from 1573.
parts.n: It must be described, not named, and must differ from the contextualization evidence.

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 1: because Columbus was writing to a crown financier to win a larger second voyage, he promised converts and gold and slaves together, so the letter shows that religion and profit were sold as one package from the start. Doc 6: recorded decades after the conquest by Nahua elders working under a Franciscan, it condemns Spanish greed, a theme friars shared, so its picture of gold-hungry conquerors fits both Nahua memory and missionary criticism of lay Spaniards.
parts.n: Each explanation must say how the sourcing affects the argument, not just identify the author, date or audience.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan how the essay shows a complex understanding.
parts.a: Argue that religious and economic motives were not rivals but reinforced each other: the Requerimiento (Doc 2) made refusing the faith the legal trigger for seizing people and land, and Sepulveda (Doc 5) turned idolatry into grounds for rule; then qualify by showing Europeans disputed this (Doc 4) and that the English version (Doc 7) used Protestantism against Spain while pursuing trade.
parts.n: Complexity must run through the argument with evidence; a closing sentence that 'it was complicated' earns nothing.

frq.title: LEQ · Contact and change in Native American societies, 1492-1607
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent to which contact with Europeans changed Native American societies in the Americas from 1492 to 1607.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: contact transformed Native societies where Spain conquered (the Caribbean, central Mexico, the Andes) through epidemics, the encomienda and mita, and missions, but most Native nations north of Mexico kept their land, government and economies to 1607, changed mainly by disease and trade goods.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('contact changed Native societies in many ways') or a claim that sets up no line of reasoning.

rows.earns: Describes the broader situation, beyond a phrase: e.g., before 1492 Native societies had adapted to diverse environments, from maize-based Pueblo and Mississippian towns to mobile Great Basin and Plains bands and salmon-rich Northwest villages, and the Aztec and Inca empires had recently built tribute states; or the Iberian background of Reconquista and Atlantic expansion.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'Native Americans lived here first' or context unconnected to the question of change.

rows.earns: 2 points: uses at least two specific pieces of evidence to support an argument about extent (e.g., the 1520 smallpox epidemic and central Mexico's population collapse; the encomienda and the Potosi mita; Catholic missions and reducciones; continuity of three-sisters farming and self-government among the Iroquois and Algonquians; Chichimeca resistance). 1 point: identifies two specific, relevant examples without using them to support an argument.
rows.loses: General statements ('many Natives died', 'the Spanish were cruel') with no specific example.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses continuity and change to frame the argument (what changed, what persisted, and why). 2 points: demonstrates a complex understanding, e.g., explains both change and continuity with regional contrast, shows Native agency (alliances, syncretism, resistance) shaping how contact changed societies, or connects the period to later developments such as the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.
rows.loses: Listing changes with no explanation of why they happened or how far they reached; a one-line nod to complexity.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Contact with Europeans transformed Native societies in the regions Spain conquered, where epidemics killed most people and the encomienda, silver mining and missions remade labor, religion and social order, but to 1607 it changed most Native nations north of Mexico only at the edges, through disease and trade goods, while their land, self-government and ways of making a living persisted.
parts.n: 'To a great extent' with no categories does not establish a line of reasoning.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the Americas in 1491: tens of millions of people in societies adapted to their environments, including maize-irrigating Pueblo towns, Mississippian chiefdoms, Eastern Woodland farming villages, mobile Great Basin and Plains bands, and Northwest villages built on salmon, alongside the young Aztec and Inca tribute empires. This baseline is what contact changed, or did not.
parts.n: Must describe, in a few sentences, the situation the essay measures change against.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
parts.a: Change, demographic: the Taino collapse on Hispaniola within a generation and central Mexico's fall from roughly 25 million to about 1 million by 1605 (a contested high estimate). Change, economic and social: the encomienda, the Potosi mita (1573), and the casta hierarchy. Change, religious: missions and reducciones, with syncretism blending Catholic and Native practice. Continuity: Iroquois and Algonquian three-sisters farming and council government, mobile Plains and Great Basin life, and forty years of Chichimeca resistance ending in Spanish gifts.
parts.n: Each piece must be specific and explicitly tied to the claim about extent.

parts.q: Row D · Analysis and reasoning: plan the reasoning and the complexity.
parts.a: Frame every paragraph as change or continuity and explain why: change was deepest where Spain found dense populations and silver, and continuity lasted where it found neither. For complexity, show Native agency shaping the outcome (Tlaxcalan alliance, syncretic religion, Chichimeca resistance) and connect forward: New Mexico's missions and labor demands led to the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, and Spanish horses would later transform Plains societies.
parts.n: The complexity must be explained with evidence; a final sentence that 'there was both change and continuity' earns nothing.

units.title: Period 2: 1607–1754
units.blurb: Jamestown tobacco, Puritan New England, Quaker Pennsylvania, the Navigation Acts, Bacon's and Stono rebellions, and the Great Awakening. Questions contrast the regions and trace the shift from servants to slavery.
keys: The Virginia Company founded Jamestown in 1607 for profit, and Rolfe's tobacco after 1612 drove land hunger and demand for labor.
Winthrop's Puritans built Massachusetts Bay in 1630 as a city upon a hill and banished dissenters Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson.
Regions diverged, from Puritan family farms to Penn's tolerant Quaker Pennsylvania and the Black-majority rice and sugar plantations.
English land hunger sparked the Pequot War (1637) and King Philip's War (1675-76), which ended Native power in southern New England.
Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 pushed Chesapeake planters from indentured servants to enslaved Africans under the 1705 slave codes.
Enslaved people resisted daily and openly, as in the 1739 Stono Rebellion that provoked South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740.
Mercantilism and the Navigation Acts bound colonial trade to England, but salutary neglect let elected assemblies run local affairs.
Whitefield's Great Awakening and Locke's Enlightenment both taught colonists to judge established authority for themselves.

topics.t: Interactions between American Indians and Europeans

excl.s: Optional Sources pages offer examples of sources appropriate for a college-level course. None of the AP Exam questions require students to have studied these specific sources.

units.check: Progress check · 20 multiple choice · 2 short answer (primary source, primary source) · 1 free response (long essay (partial))

frq.title: SAQ 1 · How did racial slavery begin in the Chesapeake? (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"In the first decades of Virginia, the planter who wanted labor looked first to England, not to Africa. English servants were cheaper, the trade in them was well established, and few men lived long enough to make a lifetime of bondage worth its higher price. Only when the flow of English servants slackened, when colonists began to outlive their terms, and when freed servants took up arms against their masters in 1676 did planters turn decisively to Africans. Racial slavery in the Chesapeake, in other words, was less an inheritance from Europe than a solution that planters arrived at, and then wrote into law, over three generations."

Martha Kellerman, historian, Tobacco and Bondage, 2016. (The historian and the book are fictional, written for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the origins of racial slavery in the Chesapeake.
parts.a: The historian argues that racial slavery in the Chesapeake was not inherited from Europe but developed gradually, over about three generations, as planters' practical answer to labor problems: when English servants grew scarcer, when servants began to survive their terms, and when armed former servants rebelled in 1676, planters turned to enslaved Africans and then wrote racial slavery into law.
parts.n: Quoting the excerpt, or writing 'the historian talks about slavery', earns nothing; state the claim, slavery as a gradual economic choice later fixed in law, in your own words.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1607 to 1754, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, supports the historian's argument.
parts.a: Anthony Johnson's career supports it. Brought to Virginia as a servant in 1621, Johnson gained his freedom, held 250 acres on the Eastern Shore by the early 1650s, and in 1655 won a court case keeping another African, John Casor, as his servant for life. That a free Black man could own land and bound laborers at mid-century shows race had not yet fixed status, as the historian argues. (Also accepted: Virginia's 1662 law making a child's status follow the mother's, showing slavery built step by step in statute; the end of the Royal African Company's monopoly in 1698, which widened the supply of captives.)
parts.n: Reusing the excerpt's own evidence (the servant supply, survival rates, 1676) earns nothing; the development must be new and explicitly tied to the argument.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1607 to 1754 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: The 1640 case of John Punch challenges it. When Punch, an African servant, ran away with two European servants, Virginia's General Court added four years to the Europeans' terms but sentenced Punch to serve for life. Englishmen already treated Africans as fit for perpetual bondage decades before the labor shift of the 1680s, so prejudice helped shape slavery rather than only following from it. (Also accepted: English planters in Barbados had built a slave society with a slave code by 1661, so Chesapeake planters adopted an existing Caribbean model rather than inventing a solution.)
parts.n: Simply disagreeing ('slavery was always about race') earns nothing; the point needs a specific development and an explanation of how it limits the historian's claim.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · An Old Light minister on the revivals (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"These itinerant preachers go from town to town without the call of any church, and the people run after them, forsaking their own settled ministers. Men of no learning, and even women and boys, now presume to exhort in public. The meetings are filled with shrieks and faintings, which the people mistake for the work of the Spirit. Congregations are torn in pieces, and neighbors call their own pastors unconverted. If every private person may judge who is saved and who may preach, what order can remain in church or in society?"

Described period document: a composite paraphrase, written for this exercise, of complaints published by Old Light ministers in New England in the early 1740s, such as the Boston minister Charles Chauncy's Seasonable Thoughts on the State of Religion in New England (1743). It is not a quotation.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which the complaint was written.
parts.a: The complaint comes from the height of the First Great Awakening in the early 1740s. George Whitefield's tours of 1739-1741 had drawn enormous crowds, and itinerant preachers such as Gilbert Tennent and James Davenport followed, often denouncing settled ministers as unconverted. Congregations in New England and the middle colonies were splitting between revival-minded New Lights and Old Lights who defended an educated, settled ministry and orderly worship.
parts.n: Summarizing what the minister says describes content, not situation; the point needs the revivals, the itinerants and the New Light-Old Light split around the text.

parts.q: Explain how the author's point of view shaped his argument.
parts.a: As an educated minister settled over a congregation, the author saw his authority, income and standing threatened by itinerants who drew his hearers away and by lay people, even women and boys, who claimed the right to exhort. That point of view explains why he treats the revival's emotion as disorder rather than grace and why he warns that private judgment endangers order in church and society: he is defending the hierarchy that placed men like him at the top.
parts.n: Identifying the author as a minister without explaining how that position shaped what he condemns earns nothing.

parts.q: Explain ONE way the Great Awakening changed colonial society in the period 1740 to 1754.
parts.a: It increased religious pluralism and weakened deference to established authority. Splits between New Lights and Old Lights produced separate congregations, a New Side-Old Side division among Presbyterians, and new colleges such as the College of New Jersey (Princeton, 1746), so no single church could speak for a colony, and colonists grew used to choosing their ministers and questioning leaders whose authority rested on learning or office. (Also accepted: the spread of evangelical Christianity among enslaved Africans; the first shared intercolonial experience.)
parts.n: 'The Great Awakening caused the Revolution' falls outside 1740-1754 and skips the mechanism; name a change inside the period.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · Who lived in the British colonies in 1750? (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the bar graph described below.

Described bar graph, titled 'Estimated Share of the Population of African Descent, Selected British Colonies, 1750'. Horizontal axis: colony, arranged from north to south and then the Caribbean. Vertical axis: percent of total population, 0 to 100. Six bars:
Colony · Estimated percent of African descent
Massachusetts · 2
Pennsylvania · 2
New York · 14
Virginia · 44
South Carolina · 61
Jamaica · 90
Source note: rounded estimates from colonial counts and historians' reconstructions (the mainland figures follow Historical Statistics of the United States). Nearly all people of African descent in these colonies were enslaved.

parts.q: Identify ONE pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: The share of people of African descent rose sharply from north to south: about 2 percent in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, 14 percent in New York, 44 percent in Virginia, 61 percent in South Carolina and about 90 percent in Jamaica, so enslaved people formed majorities only in the rice and sugar colonies.
parts.n: Reading the bars one by one without naming the trend (rising southward, majorities only in South Carolina and Jamaica) is not a pattern.

parts.q: Explain ONE cause of the pattern shown in the graph.
parts.a: Environment and crops drove it. Long growing seasons in the South and the Caribbean made labor-hungry export crops, tobacco, rice and sugar, highly profitable, so planters bought enslaved Africans in large numbers, while New England's short seasons and small family farms needed little bound labor. Rice and sugar work also killed people faster, so planters there kept importing captives, raising the share further.
parts.n: 'The South liked slavery more' names no cause; tie the percentages to crops, climate and labor demand.

parts.q: Explain ONE effect of the pattern shown in the graph on colonial society in the period 1690 to 1754.
parts.a: Where enslaved people were a majority, white fear produced the harshest laws: South Carolina adopted a Barbados-style slave code in 1696 and, after the Stono Rebellion of 1739, passed the Negro Act of 1740, which barred enslaved people from assembling, earning money and learning to write. (Also accepted: Black majorities on large, isolated rice plantations let Gullah language and African cultural practices survive in the lowcountry; New York's sizable enslaved minority helped produce the 1741 conspiracy panic and executions.)
parts.n: An effect outside the period (abolition, the Civil War) or one not tied to the population pattern earns nothing.

frq.title: DBQ · Religion and colonial society in British North America, 1630-1754
frq.stem:
Practice. The exam draws its DBQ from 1754 to 1980, so none comes from Period 2; this one practises the same seven-point skills on Period 2 content.

Evaluate the extent to which religion shaped the development of colonial society in British North America from 1630 to 1754.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; the wording is not a direct quotation.

Document 1
Source: John Winthrop, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Company, 'A Model of Christian Charity', a sermon to Puritan migrants sailing to New England, 1630.
"We have entered into a covenant with God for this work. We must be knit together as one man, delight in one another, and make one another's conditions our own, always keeping before our eyes our community as members of one body. For we must consider that we shall be as a city upon a hill; the eyes of all people are upon us. If we deal falsely with our God in this work, we shall be made a story and a byword through the world."

Document 2
Source: Massachusetts General Court, school law, 1647.
"Since it is one chief project of that old deluder, Satan, to keep men from the knowledge of the Scriptures, it is ordered that every township of fifty households shall appoint one to teach all children to write and read, and every township of one hundred households shall set up a grammar school to prepare youth for the university."

Document 3
Source: Maryland Act Concerning Religion (the Toleration Act), passed by the colony's assembly under its Catholic proprietor, Lord Baltimore, 1649.
"Whoever blasphemes God, denies our Savior Jesus Christ to be the Son of God, or denies the Holy Trinity shall be punished with death. And because forcing conscience in matters of religion has had dangerous consequences in the commonwealths where it has been practiced, no person professing to believe in Jesus Christ shall be troubled or molested for his religion or its free exercise."

Document 4
Source: Virginia General Assembly, act of 1667.
"Some doubts have arisen whether children who are slaves by birth, and who by the charity of their owners have received baptism, should be made free by it. It is enacted that baptism does not alter the condition of a person as to bondage or freedom, so that masters, freed from this doubt, may more carefully endeavor to spread Christianity among their slaves."

Document 5
Source: William Penn, proprietor of Pennsylvania, Charter of Privileges granted to the colony, 1701.
"No person who confesses one almighty God, the Creator and Ruler of the world, and who lives quietly under the civil government, shall be molested in person or estate because of his conscientious belief or practice. All persons who profess to believe in Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world, shall be capable of serving this government in any capacity."

Document 6
Source: Gilbert Tennent, Presbyterian revivalist, sermon 'The Danger of an Unconverted Ministry', preached at Nottingham, Pennsylvania, 1740.
"Unconverted ministers are like the Pharisees: they have the letter of learning but not the spirit of grace, and their preaching is cold and dead. Is it any wonder their hearers remain dead too? If people find no benefit from such a minister, they may lawfully go to hear one who has experienced the new birth, even if they must leave their own parish to do it."

Document 7
Source: Benjamin Franklin, printer and deist, Autobiography, written between 1771 and 1790, describing George Whitefield's preaching in Philadelphia in 1739.
"The multitudes of all sects and denominations who attended his sermons were enormous. It was wonderful to see the change soon made in the manners of our inhabitants: from being thoughtless or indifferent about religion, it seemed as if all the world were growing religious. I attended one sermon resolved to give nothing to his collection, and I emptied my pocket wholly into the collector's dish. I computed that he might well be heard by more than thirty thousand people."

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: religion shaped colonial society deeply at the founding of New England and Pennsylvania (Docs 1, 2, 5) and again in the Great Awakening (Docs 6, 7), but economic interest limited it where the two collided (Doc 4), and by the 1740s religion divided churches and weakened deference as much as it bound communities.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('religion shaped colonial society to a large extent'), a claim with no line of reasoning, or a thesis split between introduction and conclusion.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, beyond a phrase: e.g., the Protestant Reformation and England's religious conflicts, in which Puritans pressed by Charles I and Archbishop Laud, persecuted Quakers and English Catholics each sought American refuges; or the transatlantic evangelical movement that linked British and colonial revivals in the 1730s and 1740s.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'the colonists came for religious freedom' or context unconnected to the prompt.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument (e.g., Doc 1's covenanted community, Doc 2's Bible-reading schools, Doc 3's limited toleration with death for blasphemy, Doc 4's ruling that baptism does not free, Doc 6's call to leave unconverted ministers, Doc 7's crowds of all denominations). 1 point: accurately describes the content of three documents that address the topic.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing their content; describing fewer than three; misreading a document (e.g., treating Doc 3 as full religious freedom).

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific, described piece of evidence not in the documents and different from the context, e.g.: the banishment of Anne Hutchinson (1637-1638) or of Roger Williams, who founded Rhode Island (1636); the Halfway Covenant (1662); the Salem witch trials (1692); the founding of the College of New Jersey (Princeton, 1746) by New Light Presbyterians.
rows.loses: A name dropped without description ('Roger Williams'), evidence already in a document, or the same evidence used for contextualization.

rows.earns: For two documents, explains how or why point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience is relevant to the argument, e.g.: Doc 1's audience, migrants about to found a colony, explains its stress on unity and covenant; Doc 3's historical situation, a Catholic proprietor protecting a Catholic minority as Protestants came to outnumber them during England's civil wars, explains its narrow toleration; Doc 4's purpose, reassuring slaveholders, shows property interest setting the limits of religion; Doc 7 was written decades later by a deist who admired Whitefield's effect, so his testimony to the revival's power is notable, though memory may enlarge it.
rows.loses: Identifying the author or date ('Doc 7 is by Franklin') without explaining why that matters to the argument.

rows.earns: A complex understanding woven into the argument, e.g.: explains that religion both unified communities (Docs 1, 2) and divided them (Doc 6); shows that its influence varied by region, strong in New England and Pennsylvania and weaker than profit in the Chesapeake (Doc 4); or explains how the same Protestant conviction produced both intolerance (Hutchinson's banishment) and toleration (Docs 3, 5).
rows.loses: A single sentence noting that 'religion mattered in some colonies more than others', or a counterargument stated but not explained or tied to the thesis.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Religion shaped colonial society to a great extent where colonies were founded as religious projects, giving New England its covenanted towns and schools and Pennsylvania its toleration, and the Great Awakening spread its influence across all regions by the 1740s; but where religion collided with economic interest, as over slaves' baptism in Virginia, profit set the limits, and the revivals themselves divided churches and weakened the authority religion had once upheld.
parts.n: 'Religion and economics both mattered' does not establish a line of reasoning; say where religion's influence was strong, where it was limited, and why.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Open with England's post-Reformation religious conflict: under Charles I and Archbishop Laud, Puritans who wanted to purify the Church of England faced growing pressure, which drove the Great Migration of about 20,000 to New England in the 1630s, while Catholics, Quakers and other dissenters also looked for refuges. Colonial proprietors such as Lord Baltimore and William Penn therefore built religious aims into their charters, and later a transatlantic evangelical movement linked British and colonial revivals.
parts.n: Must describe, in several sentences, the development around the prompt and tie it to religion's role in the colonies.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan which documents support which part of the argument.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, religion as founding purpose: Doc 1 (a covenanted community meant as an example to the world) and Doc 2 (towns required to teach reading so all could know the Scriptures). Paragraph 2, toleration as policy for mixed colonies: Doc 3 (freedom for Christians, death for blasphemy) and Doc 5 (liberty of conscience for all who believe in God). Paragraph 3, limits and division: Doc 4 (baptism does not free, so property outranks faith) and Docs 6 and 7 (revivalists urging people to leave unconverted ministers; crowds of every denomination).
parts.n: Each document must be described and used for a claim, not just cited in parentheses.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece and say where it goes.
parts.a: In paragraph 1: the banishment of Anne Hutchinson (1637-1638) for teaching that the elect received grace directly, which shows how tightly the Puritan leadership enforced religious conformity in social life, including women's roles. Alternative for paragraph 3: the College of New Jersey (Princeton, 1746), founded by New Light Presbyterians, which shows the Awakening's divisions producing new institutions.
parts.n: The outside evidence must be specific, described, and different from the evidence used for context.

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 4: the Virginia assembly, made up of slaveholding planters, wrote the law to reassure masters that converting enslaved people would not cost them property, so its purpose reveals that economic interest set the boundary of religious practice. Doc 7: Franklin, a deist who did not share Whitefield's theology and wrote decades later, still recalls the revival's power and his own emptied pocket, which strengthens the claim of the Awakening's reach, though a later memoir may enlarge the numbers.
parts.n: Each sourcing point must say how the source's situation or purpose affects its use in the argument.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan how the essay shows a complex understanding.
parts.a: Argue that religion both built and broke apart colonial communities: the same Protestant conviction that knit Winthrop's covenanted towns (Docs 1, 2) produced intolerance of dissent and, a century later, revivals that split congregations and taught people to reject ministers they judged unconverted (Doc 6). Add regional variation: religion shaped New England and Pennsylvania society far more than the Chesapeake, where profit governed even baptism (Doc 4).
parts.n: The complexity must be explained with evidence across the essay; a closing sentence that 'religion had mixed effects' earns nothing.

frq.title: LEQ · The Chesapeake and New England, 1607-1700
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent of difference between the Chesapeake and New England colonies in their economic and social development from 1607 to 1700.

rows.earns: A defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: the two regions differed greatly in economy, labor and family life, because a warm tidewater suited tobacco worked by servants and then enslaved Africans while Puritan families on thin soil built farms, fisheries and trade; but they were alike in building elected self-government and in taking Native land by war.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the colonies were very different') or a claim that sets up no line of reasoning.

rows.earns: Describes the broader situation, beyond a phrase: e.g., in early 1600s England, enclosure and population growth left many poor and landless while Puritans faced rising pressure under Charles I, so joint-stock investors and religious dissenters both looked to America; or Spain's century-long head start, which showed England both the wealth and the risks of colonies.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'the English came to America in the 1600s' or context unconnected to regional difference.

rows.earns: 2 points: uses at least two specific pieces of evidence to support an argument about extent (e.g., the headright system and indentured servitude; tobacco and Bacon's Rebellion (1676); the Great Migration of families; New England's town meetings and 1647 School Law; the House of Burgesses (1619) and the Mayflower Compact; the 1622 Powhatan attack and King Philip's War). 1 point: identifies two specific, relevant examples without using them to support an argument.
rows.loses: General statements ('the South had plantations', 'Puritans were religious') with no specific example.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses comparison to frame the argument (what differed, what was alike, and why). 2 points: demonstrates a complex understanding, e.g., explains both differences and similarities with their causes, shows the regions changing over the century (the Chesapeake's sex ratio balancing and its turn to slavery; New England's growing commerce and declining zeal), or connects the contrast to the later regional divergence over slavery.
rows.loses: Two parallel descriptions with no stated similarity or difference; a one-line nod to complexity.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: The Chesapeake and New England differed to a great extent in economy, labor and family life, because the Chesapeake's long growing season and tobacco drew young single men as servants and then enslaved Africans to scattered plantations, while New England's thin soil and Puritan family migration produced compact towns, mixed farming and trade; yet both regions built elected self-government and both took Native land through war.
parts.n: 'To a great extent' with no categories or causes does not establish a line of reasoning.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe England around 1600: enclosure and population growth left many people poor and landless, joint-stock companies such as the Virginia Company pooled capital for profitable ventures, and Puritans who wanted to purify the Church of England faced rising pressure under Charles I. Profit seekers and religious dissenters left for different places, which sets up the regional contrast.
parts.n: Must describe, in a few sentences, the situation behind both migrations, not only name a date.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
parts.a: Difference, economy and labor: Chesapeake tobacco from Rolfe's 1612 crop, headrights and indentured servants, then the shift to enslaved Africans after Bacon's Rebellion (1676), versus New England's family farms, fishing, shipbuilding and West Indies trade. Difference, society: the Chesapeake's young, male, short-lived population and scattered plantations versus the Great Migration's roughly 20,000 migrants in family groups, long lives, towns and the 1647 School Law. Similarity: elected assemblies (House of Burgesses 1619; Mayflower Compact and the General Court) and wars for Native land (1622 and 1644 in Virginia; the Pequot War and King Philip's War).
parts.n: Each piece must be specific and explicitly tied to the claim about extent of difference.

parts.q: Row D · Analysis and reasoning: plan the reasoning and the complexity.
parts.a: Explain each difference by its causes: environment and crops set labor demand, and migrants' goals (profit versus a godly community) set family and town life. For complexity, show change within the century: by 1700 the Chesapeake had more native-born families and a growing enslaved labor force, while New England grew more commercial and less fervent (the Halfway Covenant, 1662). The regions converged in some ways even as slavery set them further apart.
parts.n: The complexity must be explained with evidence; a final sentence that 'there were similarities and differences' earns nothing.

units.ced: AP United States History Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2026

units.title: Period 3: 1754–1800
units.blurb: The French and Indian War, the Stamp Act, the Declaration, the Articles, the Constitutional Convention and Hamilton's plan, ending in 1800. Causation questions dominate, plus Federalist and Anti-Federalist contrasts.
keys: Britain's win in the French and Indian War (1754-1763) doubled its debt, ended salutary neglect and drew the Proclamation Line of 1763.
From the Stamp Act of 1765 to the Coercive Acts of 1774, colonists denied that a Parliament they did not elect could tax them.
Paine's Common Sense and Jefferson's Declaration of 1776 turned a tax quarrel into a Lockean rejection of monarchy itself.
Saratoga in 1777 won the French alliance whose fleet sealed Yorktown in 1781, and the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognized independence.
The Revolution brought republican motherhood and northern gradual emancipation but left southern slavery intact and women without the vote.
The Articles of Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance yet could not tax or answer Shays' Rebellion, prompting the 1787 Convention.
The Constitution balanced large and small states, counted enslaved people as three-fifths, and won ratification by promising a Bill of Rights.
Hamilton's plan split Federalists from Jeffersonian Republicans, whose feud peaked in the Alien and Sedition Acts and the Revolution of 1800.

topics.t: The Seven Years’ War (the French and Indian War)
Philosophical foundations of the American Revolution
The Constitutional Convention and debates over ratification

excl.s: Optional Sources pages offer examples of sources appropriate for a college-level course. None of the AP Exam questions require students to have studied these specific sources.

units.check: Progress check · 30 multiple choice · 2 short answer (primary source, primary source) · 1 free response (long essay (partial))

frq.title: SAQ 1 · The Revolution and slavery (secondary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"The Revolution was the first great crisis of American slavery, and slavery came out of it weaker in some places and stronger in others. In the North, the language of natural rights, the petitions of enslaved men and women, and the modest stake northern farmers and merchants had in bondage combined to set slavery on the road to extinction; by 1804 every northern state had acted against it. In Virginia and Maryland, thousands of enslaved people were freed by owners newly troubled by the contradiction between liberty and slavery. Yet the same years taught slaveholders to defend their human property in the new language of rights and to write protections for it into the nation's founding compromises. The Revolution did not so much weaken slavery as divide the nation over it."

Daniel Achterberg, historian, Liberty's Divided House, 2018. (The historian and the book are fictional, written for this exercise.)

parts.q: Describe the historian's argument about the effect of the American Revolution on slavery.
parts.a: The historian argues that the Revolution divided the nation over slavery rather than weakening it overall: revolutionary ideals, enslaved people's petitions and a small economic stake led the North to begin abolition and moved some Upper South owners to free enslaved people, while slaveholders elsewhere learned to defend slavery in the language of rights and won protections for it in the founding compromises.
parts.n: Quoting the last sentence or writing 'the historian talks about slavery' earns nothing; describe the claim, division rather than decline, in your own words.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1775 to 1800, not directly mentioned in the excerpt, supports the historian's argument.
parts.a: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) supports it. Congress banned slavery north of the Ohio River but left the lands south of the river open to it, so Kentucky (1792) and Tennessee (1796) entered the Union as slave states. That drew a geographic line between free and slave territory, the national division the historian describes. (Also accepted: the cotton gin (1793), which spread slavery into the Georgia and South Carolina backcountry while the North was ending it.)
parts.n: Reusing the excerpt's own evidence (northern abolition, Upper South manumissions, the founding compromises) earns nothing; the development must be new and tied to 'division'.

parts.q: Explain how ONE historical development from the period 1775 to 1800 could be used to challenge or modify the historian's argument.
parts.a: Enslaved people's own actions modify it. After Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) and later British offers of freedom, thousands fled to British lines, and about 3,000 Black Loyalists left New York with the British in 1783, so the sharpest wartime blow to slavery came from enslaved people and Britain, not Patriot ideals. (Also accepted: the cotton gin, an economic change rather than the Revolution, did most to entrench slavery in the Deep South.)
parts.n: Simply disagreeing ('the Revolution did weaken slavery') earns nothing; name a specific development and explain how it limits the historian's claim.

frq.title: SAQ 2 · An Anti-Federalist warning (primary source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

"Can a free republic govern a country as vast as the United States, with its millions of people of different interests and customs? History answers no. In a free republic the people must know and trust their representatives, but under this Constitution a few men, meeting far away, will make laws for the whole. The new government may lay any tax it pleases, raise armies in time of peace, and make every law it judges 'necessary and proper'. Its laws will be the supreme law of the land, and the state governments, the true guardians of our liberty, will waste away until they are nothing."

Described period document: an essay by an Anti-Federalist writing under the name 'Brutus', addressed to the citizens of New York and printed in a New York newspaper in October 1787. The wording is a paraphrase composed for this exercise from that essay's arguments; it is not a quotation.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which this essay was written.
parts.a: In September 1787 the Philadelphia Convention sent a proposed Constitution to the states, and New York, a pivotal state, began debating whether to ratify it. The Articles of Confederation had left Congress unable to tax, regulate trade or put down unrest such as Shays' Rebellion, so nationalists proposed a much stronger national government; Anti-Federalists such as 'Brutus' argued against it in newspapers, and Hamilton, Madison and Jay answered in The Federalist.
parts.n: Summarizing the excerpt ('he thinks the government is too big') describes content, not situation; the point needs the ratification contest and the Articles' failures behind it.

parts.q: Explain how the author's argument drew on ideas from the American Revolution.
parts.a: It repeats the Revolution's fear of distant, unaccountable power. Colonists had resisted Parliament because it taxed them without representation and kept a standing army among them in peacetime; 'Brutus' warns that a far-off national government will likewise 'lay any tax it pleases' and 'raise armies in time of peace', and that only governments close to the people, as the colonial assemblies had been, can protect liberty.
parts.n: Saying 'it is like the Revolution' earns nothing; name the specific revolutionary grievance (taxation without consent, standing armies, distant power) and match it to the text.

parts.q: Explain ONE way supporters of the Constitution responded to arguments like the author's between 1787 and 1791.
parts.a: Federalists promised amendments to protect rights, winning close ratification votes in Massachusetts, Virginia and New York, and the first Congress sent the states the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791; its Tenth Amendment reserved powers not delegated to the national government to the states or the people, answering the fear that the states would 'waste away'. (Also accepted: Madison's Federalist No. 10, arguing that a large republic controls faction better than a small one.)
parts.n: Naming the Bill of Rights without explaining how it answered the Anti-Federalist fear earns little; tie the response to the argument.

frq.title: SAQ 3 · 'Join, or Die' (non-text source)
frq.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the image described below.

Described image: a woodcut cartoon that Benjamin Franklin printed in his newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, on May 9, 1754, beside his report that French forces had seized the forks of the Ohio River from Virginians building a fort there. It shows a snake cut into eight pieces, each labeled with initials; from the head: 'N.E.' (New England), 'N.Y.', 'N.J.', 'P.' (Pennsylvania), 'M.' (Maryland), 'V.' (Virginia), 'N.C.', and at the tail 'S.C.' Beneath the snake are the words 'JOIN, or DIE.' A popular belief of the time held that a snake cut into pieces could come back to life if the pieces were joined before sunset.

Source: Benjamin Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 1754; image described for this exercise.

parts.q: Describe the historical situation in which Franklin published the image.
parts.a: In the spring of 1754 Britain and France were competing for the Ohio River valley: French troops had just driven Virginians from the forks of the Ohio and begun Fort Duquesne, and fighting that summer began the French and Indian War. Franklin printed the cartoon weeks before the Albany Congress, where colonial delegates met Iroquois leaders, to urge the separate, rival colonies to unite for defense against France and its Native allies.
parts.n: Describing the snake ('it shows a snake in pieces') is not the situation; the point needs the imperial contest for the Ohio valley and the call for unity it answered.

parts.q: Explain how ONE development from 1754 to 1763 shows the limits of the colonial unity the image called for.
parts.a: The Albany Plan of Union (1754), Franklin's own proposal for a colonial grand council able to raise troops and taxes for defense, was rejected by every colonial assembly, none of which would give up control over its own taxes. Throughout the war the assemblies also quarreled with one another and with British commanders over supplying men and money, so the unity the snake demanded never materialized.
parts.n: Naming the Albany Plan without saying it failed, and why, earns nothing; the point is that the colonies would not surrender local power to unite.

parts.q: Explain ONE reason colonists revived versions of this image between 1765 and 1776.
parts.a: After 1763 the threat came from Parliament rather than France: the Stamp Act (1765) taxed every colony, and the Coercive Acts (1774) showed that Britain could strip any colony of its self-government. Patriot printers reprinted the snake to argue that the colonies would fall one by one unless they resisted together, the logic behind the Stamp Act Congress and the First Continental Congress.
parts.n: 'To show unity' restates the image; the answer must name the new threat after 1763 and link the image to a specific act of joint resistance.

frq.title: DBQ · The growth of colonial resistance, 1763-1776
frq.stem:
Evaluate the relative importance of the causes of growing colonial resistance to British rule from 1763 to 1776.

The documents are paraphrased for this exercise from the sources named in each source line; the wording is not a direct quotation. Document 4 is a labelled composite.

Document 1
Source: King George III, royal proclamation issued in October 1763, after the Treaty of Paris and during Pontiac's Rebellion.
"It is just and essential to our interest and to the security of our colonies that the Indian nations under our protection not be disturbed on the lands reserved to them as hunting grounds. We therefore strictly forbid our loving subjects to settle on, or to buy from the Indians, any lands west of the sources of the rivers that flow into the Atlantic, without our special permission, and we require any who have already settled there to remove themselves."

Document 2
Source: Declaration of Rights and Grievances, adopted by delegates from nine colonies at the Stamp Act Congress in New York, October 1765, and sent to the king and both houses of Parliament.
"His Majesty's subjects in these colonies owe the same allegiance to the Crown as those born in Great Britain and are entitled to all their rights and liberties. It is essential to the freedom of a people, and the undoubted right of Englishmen, that no taxes be imposed on them without their own consent, given personally or by their representatives. The colonists are not, and from their distance cannot be, represented in the House of Commons, so no taxes can be constitutionally imposed on them except by their own legislatures."

Document 3
Source: John Dickinson, Pennsylvania lawyer, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, published in colonial newspapers in 1767-1768 in response to the Townshend duties.
"Parliament unquestionably has the right to regulate the trade of the whole empire. But these new duties are laid for the single purpose of raising money from us, not of regulating trade. If Parliament may lawfully take our money this way without our consent, our property is at its mercy, and we are slaves. Let us behave like dutiful children who have received undeserved blows from a beloved parent, and seek relief by petitions and by refusing to buy British goods."

Document 4
Source: Composite of reports printed in Boston and Providence newspapers in 1768-1769 describing 'spinning matches' held by young women who called themselves Daughters of Liberty (composed for this exercise).
"Last week forty young ladies of this town met at the minister's house at sunrise and spun from morning until evening, producing more than a hundred skeins of yarn, which they presented to the minister. They drank no foreign tea, only tea of our own country's herbs, and resolved to wear homespun rather than British cloth until the unjust revenue acts are repealed. Such industry shows that the daughters of America are no less zealous for liberty than her sons."

Document 5
Source: Paul Revere, Boston silversmith and member of the Sons of Liberty, engraving titled 'The Bloody Massacre perpetrated in King Street, Boston, on March 5th 1770', printed and sold in Boston within weeks of the event.
Described image: on the right, a straight line of British soldiers fires a volley, on the command of an officer with a raised sword, into an unarmed, orderly group of townspeople on the left, several of whom lie bleeding in the street. The building behind the soldiers, the Custom House, bears a sign reading 'Butcher's Hall'. A poem printed beneath mourns the victims and compares the soldiers to savage barbarians gloating over their prey.

Document 6
Source: Samuel Seabury, Anglican minister in New York, writing as 'A. W. Farmer', Free Thoughts on the Proceedings of the Continental Congress, a pamphlet addressed to the farmers of New York, November 1774.
"The Congress's Association, which forbids us to buy British goods and will soon forbid us to sell our produce abroad, will ruin the farmers of this province while doing Parliament little harm. Committees chosen by a handful of hotheads will pry into our houses, inspect our tea, and brand as enemies all who will not obey them. If I must be enslaved, let it be by a king at least, and not by a crowd of upstart, lawless committeemen."

Document 7
Source: Thomas Paine, recent English immigrant, Common Sense, a pamphlet published in Philadelphia in January 1776.
"The cause of America is in great measure the cause of all mankind. The very distinction between kings and subjects is contrary to nature and to scripture; one honest man is worth more to society than all the crowned ruffians who ever lived. Since the blood shed at Lexington, reconciliation is a foolish dream. There is something absurd in supposing that a continent should be governed forever by an island. Nothing can settle our affairs so quickly as an open and determined declaration of independence."

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: The most important cause of growing resistance was the constitutional principle that Parliament could not tax colonists without their consent (Docs 2, 3), which boycotts and crowd action turned into a popular movement (Docs 4, 5); British coercion after 1773 then pushed resistance toward independence and an attack on monarchy itself (Doc 7), while western land restrictions (Doc 1) angered settlers and speculators but mattered less.
parts.n: A thesis that lists causes ('taxes, the Proclamation, and the Boston Massacre caused resistance') does not weigh them; the prompt asks for relative importance, so rank them.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Open with the Seven Years' War: Britain's victory doubled its national debt and left it a vast territory to garrison, so ministers ended salutary neglect and looked to the colonies for revenue. Add that colonists, after decades of self-rule through elected assemblies and steeped in English rights and Enlightenment ideas of consent, no longer needed British protection against France.
parts.n: Two or three sentences that describe developments and connect them to the prompt; 'tensions were rising' or a bare date earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence from the documents: plan which documents support which part of the argument.
parts.a: Paragraph 1, constitutional principle as the core cause: Doc 2 (only colonial legislatures may tax), Doc 3 (revenue duties are unconstitutional even while trade regulation is accepted). Paragraph 2, popular mobilization: Doc 4 (women's homespun boycott), Doc 5 (propaganda turning the shooting into a massacre). Paragraph 3, escalation to independence: Doc 7 (monarchy itself rejected after Lexington), with Doc 6 showing resistance splitting colonists. Doc 1 as a secondary, regional grievance.
parts.n: Describe each document's content in your own words and tie it to the claim; a list of document numbers or long quotations earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents: choose one piece and say where it goes.
parts.a: In paragraph 3: the Coercive Acts (1774), which closed Boston's port and rewrote the Massachusetts charter after the Tea Party, persuaded other colonies that any charter could be revoked and led twelve colonies to send delegates to the First Continental Congress. Alternative for paragraph 2: the Sons of Liberty's 1765 crowd actions forcing stamp distributors such as Andrew Oliver to resign.
parts.n: It must be described, not just named, and must differ from the evidence used for contextualization (the war debt).

parts.q: Row D · Sourcing: plan two sourcing explanations.
parts.a: Doc 5: Revere, a Son of Liberty, made the engraving to sell and to rouse Bostonians against the troops, so it shows a calm crowd and an ordered volley and omits the taunts and thrown objects described at the trials; its value is as evidence of how Patriots used propaganda to widen resistance. Doc 6: Seabury, an Anglican Loyalist writing to New York farmers, stresses the boycott's cost and committee coercion to peel farmers away from Congress, which shows that resistance was contested, not unanimous.
parts.n: Each explanation must say how the point of view, purpose, audience or situation affects the argument, not just identify who wrote it and when.

parts.q: Row D · Complexity: plan how the essay shows a complex understanding.
parts.a: Show change over time in the causes: from 1765 to 1768 colonists professed loyalty and objected only to taxation (Docs 2, 3), but by 1774-1776 coercion and bloodshed turned a tax dispute into a rejection of monarchy (Doc 7). Qualify with Doc 6: resistance also divided colonists, so the 'causes' of resistance were also causes of a civil conflict among Americans.
parts.n: Complexity must run through the argument with evidence; a closing line that 'there were many causes' earns nothing.

rows.earns: A defensible claim that weighs causes and sets up a line of reasoning, in one place, e.g.: the constitutional objection to taxation without consent (Docs 2, 3) drove resistance, popular boycotts and propaganda spread it (Docs 4, 5), and British coercion after 1773 turned it toward independence (Doc 7), while the Proclamation line (Doc 1) was a lesser, regional grievance.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('there were many causes of resistance'), listing causes without ranking them, or a thesis split between introduction and conclusion.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, beyond a phrase: e.g., the Seven Years' War's debt and new territory ending salutary neglect; or the colonial tradition of self-rule through elected assemblies and English and Enlightenment ideas of consent.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'after the French and Indian War' with no description, or context unconnected to colonial resistance.

rows.r: Row C · Evidence from the documents
rows.earns: 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about relative importance (e.g., Doc 2's claim that only colonial legislatures may tax; Doc 3's line between trade regulation and revenue; Doc 4's homespun boycott; Doc 7's attack on monarchy). 1 point: accurately describes the content of three documents that address the topic.
rows.loses: Quoting or listing documents without describing them; describing fewer than three; misreading a document (e.g., treating Doc 6 as Patriot or Doc 1 as a tax).

rows.r: Row C · Evidence beyond the documents
rows.earns: One specific, described piece of evidence not in the documents and different from the context, e.g.: the Coercive Acts (1774); the Boston Tea Party (1773) and the Tea Act behind it; Sons of Liberty crowd actions against stamp distributors (1765); the Committees of Correspondence; Lexington and Concord (April 1775).
rows.loses: A name dropped without description ('the Tea Party'), evidence already in a document, or the same evidence used for contextualization.

rows.earns: For two documents, explains how or why point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience is relevant to the argument, e.g.: Doc 5's propaganda purpose; Doc 6's Loyalist, Anglican point of view and farmer audience; Doc 2's audience of king and Parliament explaining its loyal tone; Doc 3's moderate purpose shaping its call for petitions and boycotts rather than force; Doc 7's mass audience explaining its plain style.
rows.loses: Identifying the author or date ('Doc 3 was written by Dickinson in 1768') without explaining why that matters to the argument.

rows.earns: A complex understanding woven into the argument, e.g.: explains how the causes changed from 1765 to 1776 (tax principle to rejection of monarchy); weighs primary against secondary causes with evidence; or uses Doc 6 and Loyalist evidence to show that resistance divided colonists.
rows.loses: A single sentence saying 'the causes were complicated', or a counterargument stated but not explained or tied to the thesis.

frq.title: LEQ · Foreign affairs and the first party system, 1789-1800
frq.stem: Evaluate the extent to which foreign affairs shaped the development of the first political parties from 1789 to 1800.

parts.q: Row A · Thesis: write a thesis for this prompt.
parts.a: Foreign affairs did not create the first parties, which began in the domestic fight over Hamilton's financial program and the meaning of the Constitution, but from 1793 to 1800 the war between Britain and revolutionary France turned that dispute into organized, national parties, as neutrality, Jay's Treaty and the XYZ Affair forced choices that led to the Alien and Sedition Acts and the election of 1800.
parts.n: 'To a great extent' with no categories does not establish a line of reasoning; say what foreign affairs did and did not do.

parts.q: Row B · Contextualization: plan the context paragraph.
parts.a: Describe the founders' hostility to faction (Madison's Federalist No. 10, Washington's hopes for a government above party) and the ratification contest of 1787-1788 between Federalists and Anti-Federalists, which left unresolved how strong the national government should be. Add that the French Revolution, begun in 1789, and the European war from 1793 put the young, weak nation between two empires that controlled its trade.
parts.n: Must describe, in a few sentences, the setting the parties grew from; a phrase such as 'the new nation was divided' earns nothing.

parts.q: Row C · Evidence: plan the body paragraphs and their evidence.
