cards.q: Classify each development under the Period 2 key concept the CED places it in, with a phrase of reasoning: KC-2.1 (colonization patterns and competition for resources) or KC-2.2 (exchanges with Britain that bound the colonies to it and bred resistance): the headright system · the Great Awakening · the Pueblo Revolt · the Navigation Acts · New France's fur trade · the Virginia slave codes of 1705 · King Philip's War · the Zenger trial · South Carolina's rice plantations · the Dominion of New England · the Beaver Wars · the consumer revolution
cards.a:
headright system → KC-2.1 (the Chesapeake's land-and-labor pattern)
Great Awakening → KC-2.2 (transatlantic religious exchange that also taught independence of mind)
Pueblo Revolt → KC-2.1 (Native resistance to Spanish colonizing goals)
Navigation Acts → KC-2.2 (Britain's mercantilist imperial structure)
New France's fur trade → KC-2.1 (the French trade-and-alliance model)
Virginia slave codes of 1705 → KC-2.2 (the colonies' system of slavery, KC-2.2.II)
King Philip's War → KC-2.1 (English-Native conflict over land)
Zenger trial → KC-2.2 (evolving ideas of liberty and print culture)
South Carolina rice plantations → KC-2.1 (a regional economy shaped by environment)
Dominion of New England → KC-2.2 (imperial control and colonial resistance)
Beaver Wars → KC-2.1 (competition over resources among Native nations and European rivals)
consumer revolution → KC-2.2 (Anglicization through transatlantic trade)
cards.h: → key concept + a phrase of reasoning, each item
cards.n: The CED files slavery's legal system under KC-2.2 (KC-2.2.II), not KC-2.1. A bare label with no reason earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain why the British colonies in 1754 were both more closely tied to Britain and more self-governing than they had been a century earlier.
cards.a: Trade and self-rule grew together. Rising exports, British credit, consumer goods, print and revivals bound colonists to Britain, while salutary neglect let their assemblies control taxes and officials' pay. Colonists grew more British in culture just as they grew used to governing themselves.
cards.h: → trade, goods, print bind colonies to Britain → lax enforcement lets assemblies rule → ties and autonomy grow together
cards.n: Treating closer ties and self-rule as a contradiction to choose between earns nothing; KC-2.2 says the same exchanges did both.
o: The consumer revolution made colonists British in taste, while decades of assemblies controlling the purse made them expect British liberties at home.
The Great Awakening and the Enlightenment both crossed the Atlantic from Britain, yet both taught colonists to judge authority for themselves.

w.a: By 1754 the colonies were already trying to break away from Britain.
w.why: anachronism; independence was not sought until 1775-1776

w.a: The colonies were closer to Britain because it enforced its laws strictly after 1700.
w.why: false; enforcement was lax under salutary neglect

w.a: Both happened because the colonies were far from Britain.
w.why: distance explains autonomy but not the closer ties

cards.q: Explain why elected self-government persisted in the British colonies from 1619 to 1754 even as their economies and labor systems changed.
cards.a: Its causes never went away. Britain stayed distant and, apart from the Dominion of New England (1686-1689), inattentive; charters and English law gave colonists a claim to representative assemblies; and wide landownership made many white men voters. So assemblies kept control of taxes while labor shifted to slavery.
cards.h: → distance + lax oversight + English rights + wide landownership → assemblies endure while economies change
cards.n: Saying assemblies continued without saying why earns nothing; a continuity is an argument too and needs its causes.
o: The one serious attempt to abolish colonial assemblies, the Dominion of New England, collapsed in 1689, which shows how entrenched self-rule had become.
Colonial elites, whether New England town leaders or Virginia planters, controlled the assemblies and had every reason to defend them.

w.a: Self-government persisted because Britain wanted the colonies to be democratic.
w.why: misreads motive; Britain tolerated autonomy out of neglect and convenience

w.a: Self-government persisted because every colonist could vote.
w.why: false; women, the enslaved, servants and the propertyless could not

w.a: Self-government stayed the same because nothing changed in Period 2.
w.why: denies obvious change and gives no cause

cards.q: Explain why 1754, rather than 1763 or 1776, marks the end of Period 2.
cards.a: In 1754 imperial rivalry became the war that remade the colonial relationship. Fighting in the Ohio valley began the French and Indian War; its debts and victory led Britain to end salutary neglect after 1763, which drove Period 3's crisis. Earlier imperial wars had left the colonial system intact.
cards.h: → Ohio valley clash → war for the continent → debts and reforms → end of salutary neglect → imperial crisis
cards.n: Saying 'the French and Indian War started in 1754' restates the date; the point is the chain from that war to the end of salutary neglect.
o: King William's, Queen Anne's and King George's Wars ended without changing how Britain governed its colonies; the war that began in 1754 did.
1763 is an effect, not the turning point itself: the Proclamation Line and new taxes follow from the war that began in 1754.

w.a: Period 2 ends in 1754 because that is when the Revolution began.
w.why: wrong; the Revolutionary War began in 1775

w.a: 1754 was chosen because the colonies declared independence that year.
w.why: false; independence was declared in 1776

w.a: Period 2 ends in 1754 because Britain first taxed the colonies that year.
w.why: wrong; the Sugar and Stamp Acts came in 1764-1765

cards.q: Explain why competition over resources among Europeans and American Indians intensified between 1607 and 1754.
cards.a: More people wanted the same land and furs. British colonists multiplied past a million and pushed west, France ringed them with posts from Quebec to New Orleans, and Native nations, shrunk by epidemics, fought to keep hunting grounds and trade. By the 1750s all three claimed the Ohio valley.
cards.h: → British population boom + French posts + Native nations defending land and trade → rival claims meet in Ohio valley
cards.n: Naming the French and Indian War answers a different question; explain the rising pressure that made the Ohio valley a flashpoint.
o: The fur and deerskin trades depleted animals, so nations and their European partners competed for new hunting grounds farther west.
Imperial wars from 1689 to 1748 were fought partly in America, and each one sharpened rivalry over borders and Native alliances.

w.a: Competition grew because Europeans stopped trading with Native nations.
w.why: false; trade expanded

w.a: Competition grew because Spain controlled the Ohio valley.
w.why: false; France and Britain contested it

w.a: Competition eased after 1700 because everyone had enough land.
w.why: contradicts the rising conflict of the period

cards.q: Date the founding of Jamestown and name the company that financed it.
cards.a: 1607, by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company whose investors expected profit from gold, trade or crops. Early Jamestown nearly failed: disease, famine (the 'starving time' of 1609-1610) and conflict with the Powhatan killed most settlers until tobacco gave the colony a paying export.
cards.h: → year + sponsor + motive
cards.n: Naming the crown or the Pilgrims as the sponsor loses the point; profit, not religion, launched the Chesapeake, the standard contrast with New England.

cards.q: Describe how Spain colonized North America north of Mexico between 1607 and 1754.
cards.a: Spain held its northern borderlands with a thin chain of missions, presidios (forts) and small towns rather than a large settler population. Franciscan friars gathered Native people into missions in Florida and New Mexico to convert them and use their labor; Santa Fe (about 1610) governed New Mexico; and Spain pushed into Texas from 1690, and for good after 1716, to block the French. These were defensive and missionary frontiers, not sources of silver.
cards.h: → institutions + where + purpose
cards.n: Describing Spanish North America as a silver colony earns nothing; the silver came from Mexico and Peru, and the borderlands were buffers held by missions and forts.

cards.q: Identify Fort Mose and explain what it shows about Spanish colonial society.
cards.a: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose, founded in 1738 near St. Augustine, Florida, was the first legally sanctioned free Black town in what became the United States. Spain had promised freedom (by a 1693 decree) to enslaved people who fled the English colonies and accepted Catholicism, and it armed Fort Mose's men as a militia. It shows Spain incorporating free Africans into its colonial society while using them against British rivals.
cards.h: → what and when + who lived there + what it shows
cards.n: Calling Spain antislavery earns nothing: Spain held slaves too, and offered freedom to weaken the Carolinas. Stono's rebels (1739) marched toward Florida.
x: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose

cards.q: Identify New France and its fur-trade-based economy.
cards.a: New France was France's colony along the St. Lawrence River, founded at Quebec by Samuel de Champlain in 1608 and later stretched through the Great Lakes to Louisiana. It stayed thinly settled and lived by the fur trade, which depended on alliances with Native peoples such as the Huron (Wendat) and Algonquins, on intermarriage and on Jesuit missions rather than on large farms.
cards.h: → where + founded when + what its economy rested on
cards.n: Describing New France as a farming settler colony like Virginia earns nothing; it had few colonists and needed Native hunters and allies, not their land.

cards.q: Define coureurs des bois and explain their role in New France.
cards.a: Coureurs des bois ('runners of the woods') were French traders who went into the interior to trade directly with Native hunters, often living in Native villages and marrying Native women. They carried the fur trade west, built the kinship ties that anchored French-Native alliances, and began mixed-ancestry (Métis) families.
cards.h: → who they were + what they did + the result
cards.n: Intermarriage here was a trade strategy, not proof of French tolerance; marrying into Native kin networks secured furs and allies.

cards.q: Identify La Salle's claim of Louisiana and the French expansion that followed.
cards.a: In 1682 Rene-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, traveled down the Mississippi to its mouth and claimed the whole river basin for Louis XIV as Louisiana. France followed with Gulf coast posts from 1699 and New Orleans in 1718, linking Canada to the Gulf by a chain of forts and trading posts. That arc of French posts hemmed the British colonies in behind the Appalachians.
cards.h: → who, when, what he claimed + what France built after
cards.n: Few French settlers followed; the claim was held by forts, traders and Native allies, which is why it collided with British land hunger in the Ohio valley.

cards.q: Identify Henry Hudson's 1609 voyage and the claim it gave the Dutch.
cards.a: In 1609 the English navigator Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company in search of a Northwest Passage to Asia, explored the river later named for him. His voyage gave the Dutch their claim to the Hudson valley, where they built the fur-trading colony of New Netherland, with Fort Orange (Albany) upriver trading with the Mohawk.
cards.h: → his sponsor + what he explored + the claim it created
cards.n: Hudson was English but sailed for the Dutch; calling it an English claim loses the point. The CED names no explorers, so this card is illustrative.

cards.q: Identify New Netherland and New Amsterdam.
cards.a: New Netherland was the Dutch colony along the Hudson River, run by the Dutch West India Company (chartered 1621) chiefly for the fur trade, with its capital at New Amsterdam on Manhattan. It stayed small, relied on trade with the Mohawk and other Native peoples, and was unusually diverse in religion and origin; large 'patroon' estates along the Hudson were the company's attempt to attract farmers.
cards.h: → who ran it + economy + main traits
cards.n: Treating it as a religious refuge loses the point; it was a trading company's colony whose diversity came from commerce.

cards.q: Date the English seizure of New Netherland and its renaming as New York.
cards.a: 1664. An English fleet sent by James, Duke of York, took New Amsterdam without a fight, and colony and city were renamed New York. The Dutch retook it briefly in 1673 but returned it by treaty in 1674. The conquest closed the gap between New England and the Chesapeake and left New York with Dutch landholding and an unusually mixed population.
cards.h: → year + how + what it changed
cards.n: Saying the Dutch sold the colony, or dating the takeover to the 1700s, earns nothing; it was a conquest in the Anglo-Dutch commercial wars.

cards.q: Contrast Dutch and French colonization with English colonization in settler population and land use.
cards.a: The Dutch and French built trading colonies with few settlers that depended on Native partners for furs, so they sought Native cooperation, gave gifts and intermarried. The English sent far more settlers, including whole families, who wanted farmland, so they took Native land and lived apart from Native peoples. Each pattern followed from what the colony needed from Native people: trade and alliance, or land.
cards.h: → settler numbers + land use + what each needed from Natives
cards.n: Calling the French 'kinder' earns nothing; the difference came from the fur trade's need for Native partners versus English farms' need for land.

cards.q: Identify the motives that drew English migrants to the colonies, as the CED lists them.
cards.a: The CED names four: social mobility, economic prosperity, religious freedom and improved living conditions. Poor young men went to the Chesapeake hoping for land after serving indentures; Puritan families went to New England to worship as they chose; Quakers and others found toleration in Pennsylvania; and many simply left England's crowded, landless countryside. Women as well as men came, in far larger numbers than to New France or New Netherland.
cards.h: → the four motives + a region that shows each
cards.n: 'They came for religious freedom' alone falls short: most English migrants, especially to the Chesapeake, came for land and work.

cards.q: State the approximate number of Puritans who migrated to New England during the Great Migration.
cards.a: About 20,000 English Puritans migrated to New England between 1630 and the early 1640s, when the English Civil War halted the flow. They came mostly in family groups, with many women and children, so New England afterward grew mainly by natural increase rather than by new immigration.
cards.h: → a number + a date range + how they came
cards.n: The figure is an estimate. Confusing it with the twentieth-century Great Migration of Black Americans (Period 7) is a common slip.

cards.q: Define a redemptioner.
cards.a: A redemptioner was a migrant, usually German, who crossed the Atlantic on credit and on arrival had a short time to find relatives or an employer to 'redeem' the fare; if not, the captain sold the migrant's labor for a term of years. Unlike standard indentures signed in Europe, the terms were set after landing, often in Philadelphia, and families sometimes bargained together.
cards.h: → who + how the fare was paid + contrast with indenture
cards.n: Treating redemptioners as enslaved loses the point; like indentured servants they were bound for a term, not for life.

cards.q: Identify the German and Scots-Irish immigrants who settled the Middle Colonies and backcountry.
cards.a: Germans, many from the Rhineland and the Palatinate, came from the early 1700s to farm southeastern Pennsylvania, becoming the 'Pennsylvania Dutch' (from Deutsch). Scots-Irish Presbyterians from Ulster came in large numbers after about 1717 and pushed onto the frontier, from Pennsylvania down the Great Wagon Road into Virginia and the Carolinas. Together they made the middle colonies and the backcountry the most ethnically mixed parts of British America.
cards.h: → each group + origin + where it settled
cards.n: The 'Pennsylvania Dutch' were German, not Dutch; confusing them with New Netherland's settlers earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain the push and pull factors that drew German and Scots-Irish migrants to the colonial backcountry in the early eighteenth century.
cards.a: Push: war, religious persecution and hard winters and harvests in the German Rhineland and Palatinate; rising rents, drought and legal limits on Presbyterians in Ulster. Pull: cheap, fertile land and religious toleration in Pennsylvania, advertised by promoters and by letters home from earlier migrants. Both groups then moved west and south down the Great Wagon Road, settling the backcountry and pressing on Native lands.
cards.h: → push factors, pull factors, the result of their settlement
cards.n: A list of pushes and pulls with no link to where the migrants settled falls short; name the pull that explains Pennsylvania and the backcountry.

cards.q: Classify each feature as Spanish, French, Dutch, or English colonization in North America (1607-1754), with a phrase of reasoning: missions and presidios · coureurs des bois · patroon estates · headright grants · the Great Migration of Puritan families · the fur post at Fort Orange · Franciscan friars among the Pueblos · Jesuit missions among the Huron · town meetings · Fort Mose · forts along the Mississippi · a Quaker proprietary colony
cards.a:
missions and presidios → Spanish (borderlands held by friars and soldiers, not settlers)
coureurs des bois → French (traders living among Native hunters)
patroon estates → Dutch (the West India Company's lure for farmers on the Hudson)
headright grants → English (land for importing laborers to the Chesapeake)
Great Migration of Puritan families → English (family settlement of New England)
Fort Orange → Dutch (Hudson River fur trade with the Mohawk)
Franciscans among the Pueblos → Spanish (conversion and labor in New Mexico)
Jesuits among the Huron → French (missions that followed the fur trade)
town meetings → English (New England self-government)
Fort Mose → Spanish (free Black town and militia in Florida)
Mississippi forts → French (Louisiana's chain of posts)
Quaker proprietary colony → English (Penn's Pennsylvania)
cards.h: → empire + a phrase of reasoning, each item
cards.n: Jesuits worked for France among the Huron and Franciscans for Spain among the Pueblos; mixing up the two orders is the usual slip.

cards.q: Explain why New France depended on alliances with American Indians far more than the English colonies did.
cards.a: New France lived on furs that Native hunters trapped and traded, and it had few colonists to farm or fight. So France needed Native partners, not Native land: it sealed trade with gifts, intermarriage and military alliance, and relied on Native allies in its wars against the Iroquois and the English.
cards.h: → fur economy needs Native hunters + few French settlers → gifts, intermarriage, alliance → allied warfare
cards.n: 'The French were friendlier' earns nothing without the cause: the fur trade and a tiny settler population made alliance a necessity.
o: English farmers wanted Native land and could replace Native labor with servants and slaves, so they needed few Native allies.
With only a few thousand colonists in the 1660s, New France could not defend itself without allies such as the Huron and Algonquins.

w.a: The French relied on alliances because they respected Native culture more than the English did.
w.why: sentiment, not cause; the fur economy made alliance necessary

w.a: The French relied on alliances because Native people converted to Catholicism.
w.why: conversion was partial and followed trade; it explains nothing

w.a: New France had no army, so it had to be friendly.
w.why: false; France sent troops, and the fur trade is the cause

cards.q: Explain why English colonization attracted far more migrants than New France or New Netherland.
cards.a: England had more people to spare and more reasons to leave: poverty after enclosure, and dissenters the crown let go. Its colonies offered land through headrights and cheap sales. France barred Huguenots from New France and offered fur work in a cold climate; the prosperous Dutch had little reason to leave.
cards.h: → English push (poverty, dissent) + pull (land) vs French and Dutch limits → far larger English migration
cards.n: Pointing only to religion misses the main pull, land; a comparison needs the reason on both sides.
o: The English crown let Puritans and Quakers leave, while France excluded its Protestant minority from New France after 1627, cutting off a ready pool of migrants.
English colonies promised ownership of farmland, while New France's seigneurial landholding and fur economy offered a would-be landowner little.

w.a: More English came because England had a bigger navy.
w.why: naval power does not explain who wanted to emigrate

w.a: The English colonies had better weather than New France.
w.why: partly true of Canada but ignores New Netherland and gives no push

w.a: The French and Dutch were not interested in North America.
w.why: false; both held and defended colonies there for decades

cards.q: Explain why Spain's northern borderlands held few settlers compared with the English colonies.
cards.a: North of Mexico Spain found no silver and few tribute-payers, so it held Florida, New Mexico and Texas as defensive and missionary frontiers. The crown paid for missions and presidios, not mass settlement, and migrants preferred richer Mexico. Distance, dry land and the Pueblo Revolt raised the cost.
cards.h: → no silver, few tribute-payers → frontier held for defense and conversion → missions and forts, not settlers
cards.n: Saying Spain 'lost interest' earns nothing; the borderlands' purpose, buffer and mission field, did not need many colonists.
o: Spanish wealth came from Mexican and Peruvian silver and Native labor, so emigrants went there; the northern frontier offered neither.
The borderlands existed to guard the silver fleets' route and block French and English rivals, jobs a few forts and missions could do.

w.a: Spain had few settlers because it lost its colonies after the Pueblo Revolt.
w.why: false; Spain retook New Mexico in 1692 and kept Florida

w.a: Spanish people did not like to emigrate.
w.why: false; hundreds of thousands went to Mexico and Peru

w.a: Spain only cared about gold, so it ignored North America.
w.why: too blunt; Spain deliberately held the borderlands

cards.q: Explain why German and Scots-Irish migrants settled mainly in Pennsylvania and the backcountry rather than in New England.
cards.a: Pennsylvania offered what they sought: toleration for all Christians, cheap fertile land on easy terms, and a busy port, Philadelphia, where ships landed. New England's towns had taken up the good land and supported a Congregational establishment, so later newcomers moved west and then south along the backcountry.
cards.h: → toleration + cheap land + Philadelphia's port → Pennsylvania; New England's land taken, church set → backcountry
cards.n: A list of push factors from Europe answers a different question; this one needs the pull that sorted migrants into Pennsylvania rather than New England.
o: Some Scots-Irish did go to New England around 1718, but town land was scarce and Boston was unwelcoming, so most later migrants chose Pennsylvania.
Penn's promotional tracts, translated into German and Dutch in the 1680s, pointed continental migrants toward Philadelphia from the start.

w.a: They settled in Pennsylvania because it was the only colony that accepted immigrants.
w.why: false; other colonies admitted them too

w.a: They avoided New England because it was too cold to farm.
w.why: New Englanders farmed; the issue was scarce land and an established church

w.a: They went to Pennsylvania because the Quakers paid their passage.
w.why: false; most paid their own way or came as redemptioners

cards.q: Explain why the Dutch lost New Netherland to England in 1664.
cards.a: New Netherland was small and weakly defended: the West India Company cared about trade more than settlers, so under 10,000 colonists faced tens of thousands in New England. In the Anglo-Dutch commercial wars England wanted the Hudson's trade and the gap in its coast, and Stuyvesant surrendered without a fight.
cards.h: → company invests little in settlers → small, weak colony → English commercial rivalry → surrender without a fight
cards.n: Saying the Dutch 'sold' New York (a mix-up with the 1626 Manhattan purchase) earns nothing; weak settlement met English commercial rivalry.
o: The colony's varied, discontented residents, including English settlers on Long Island, had little reason to fight for the Company.
England's Navigation Acts targeted Dutch shipping, so taking New Netherland removed a Dutch trading base inside England's American coast.

w.a: The Dutch lost New Netherland because Native nations drove them out.
w.why: false; the English took it

w.a: The Dutch gave it up because they had no interest in trade.
w.why: false; the colony existed for trade

w.a: The Dutch lost it in the French and Indian War.
w.why: wrong war, nearly a century early

cards.q: Define the headright system.
cards.a: The headright system granted land, typically 50 acres a head in Virginia, to whoever paid a migrant's passage, including the planter who imported indentured servants. It turned the servant trade into a road to landholding for planters, so large estates grew in a few hands while freed servants found little good land left.
cards.h: → what was granted + to whom + the effect on landholding
cards.n: Saying the servant received the headright is the trap: the land went to whoever paid the passage, usually the planter, which concentrated landholding.

cards.q: Define indentured servitude.
cards.a: Indentured servitude was a contract in which a migrant, usually a poor young Englishman, traded four to seven years of unpaid labor for passage to America, food and shelter, plus 'freedom dues' such as tools, clothes or corn at the end. Servants were bound but not owned for life, and they could appeal to courts. Such servants did most Chesapeake tobacco work before about 1680.
cards.h: → the contract + its terms + who served + where
cards.n: Indenture was a status one left; slavery became lifelong, hereditary and racial. Calling servants 'slaves' blurs the contrast the exam tests.

cards.q: Identify the author's claim in this excerpt and one piece of evidence the author uses. (Composite paraphrase of 1650s promotional pamphlets for Virginia, written for this deck: 'Let no man believe the slanders that Virginia is a grave for Englishmen. The country is now healthful for those who are careful in their first summer; the soil yields tobacco and corn in plenty; and a servant who serves out his time honestly receives his corn and clothes and may take up land of his own. I know many who came over as servants and now keep servants of their own.')
cards.a: Claim: Virginia is now a healthy land of opportunity where a hardworking servant can rise to own land. Evidence: the author cites fertile soil yielding tobacco and corn, the freedom dues and land open to servants who finish their terms, and his own knowledge of former servants who now keep servants. Written to recruit migrants, it plays down the high death rates and shrinking supply of good land in the 1650s Chesapeake.
cards.h: → the claim in your own words + one piece of its evidence
cards.n: Copying a sentence of the excerpt is not identifying its claim; paraphrase the argument. The pamphlet is a composite written for this deck, not a real quotation.

cards.q: Identify the House of Burgesses and give its founding year.
cards.a: The House of Burgesses, which first met at Jamestown in 1619, was the first elected representative assembly in English America. Its members, chosen by free men (from 1670 only property holders could vote), made local laws with the governor and council; it survived Virginia's conversion to a royal colony in 1624 and became the planters' voice, above all over taxation.
cards.h: → year + what it was + who held power in it
cards.n: 1619 is a triple date: the Burgesses, the first recorded Africans at Point Comfort, and a shipment of women settlers. Calling it a full democracy overstates it.

cards.q: Compare how political power was exercised in New England and in the southern colonies before 1754.
cards.a: Similarity: both regions had elected assemblies that were unusually democratic for the era, because distance and Britain's lax attention left colonists to govern themselves. Difference: New England towns ran local affairs through participatory town meetings, which also chose members of the colonial legislature, while in the South wealthy planters held local authority as justices and militia officers and dominated the elected assemblies, with ordinary voters deferring to them.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference + the reason
cards.n: Calling either region fully democratic earns nothing: voters were free white men, usually property holders, and southern voters deferred to the planter gentry.

cards.q: Identify the Pilgrims and the Mayflower Compact.
cards.a: The Pilgrims were Separatists who had broken with the Church of England; they landed at Plymouth in 1620. Lacking a charter for that site, the men aboard the Mayflower signed the Mayflower Compact, agreeing to form a 'civil body politic' and to obey laws made for the general good. It is an early example of government by consent.
cards.h: → who they were + where and when + what the compact did
cards.n: The compact was not a constitution or a grant of religious freedom; overstating it earns nothing. Pair it with the House of Burgesses on self-government.

cards.q: Identify the founding of Massachusetts Bay Colony.
cards.a: Massachusetts Bay was founded in 1630 when roughly a thousand Puritans led by John Winthrop arrived, beginning the Great Migration. Unlike Plymouth's Separatists, they meant to purify the Church of England from within, and they built a Bible commonwealth centered on Boston, governed through a General Court elected by male church members and through town meetings.
cards.h: → year + leader + purpose + how it was governed
cards.n: Confusing it with Plymouth, or saying it offered religious freedom, loses the point; it tolerated no dissent, as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson found.

cards.q: Explain what John Winthrop meant by a 'city upon a hill.'
cards.a: Winthrop meant that the Puritan colony, bound in a covenant with God, would be watched by the world, so its success or failure would honor or disgrace God and the cause of reform. In his 1630 sermon 'A Model of Christian Charity' he urged settlers to put the community's good above private gain. It was a warning of obligation, not a boast of superiority.
cards.h: → what he meant + where he said it + warning vs boast
cards.n: Classic sourcing trap: later politicians used the phrase as national boasting; Winthrop meant scrutiny and duty for a religious community.

cards.q: Contrast Separatists and non-separating Puritans.
cards.a: Separatists, such as Plymouth's Pilgrims, judged the Church of England beyond saving and left it entirely. Non-separating Puritans, who founded Massachusetts Bay, stayed formally within the Church of England and aimed to reform it by building a purified model community. Both were Calvinists who wanted their own godly communities, not religious toleration for others.
cards.h: → each group's view of the English church + a shared trait
cards.n: Saying either group sought religious freedom for all earns nothing; each wanted freedom to practice its own faith, and Massachusetts punished dissent.

cards.q: Identify the Massachusetts School Law of 1647 (the 'Old Deluder Satan' Act).
cards.a: The Massachusetts School Law of 1647 required every town of 50 families to appoint a teacher of reading and writing and every town of 100 families to keep a grammar school. Its preamble named the aim: to thwart 'that old deluder, Satan', who kept people from knowing the Scriptures. It helped give New England the highest literacy rate in the colonies.
cards.h: → year + what it required + why
cards.n: Its purpose was Bible reading, not democratic citizenship, though it is an ancestor of public schooling. The CED does not name it, so it is illustrative.

cards.q: Define the putting-out system of colonial household production.
cards.a: The putting-out system organized production by having merchants supply raw materials, such as wool, flax or cut leather, to rural households that spun, wove or stitched them at home for piece rates. In the colonies it stayed small before 1754, beside the household making of cloth and tools for family use in New England's mixed economy; it spread mainly later in the century, as in shoemaking around Lynn, Massachusetts.
cards.h: → who supplied what + who did the work + where and when
cards.n: Illustrative; the KCs do not name it. Picturing large colonial putting-out networks before 1754 overstates it; most household making was for family use.

cards.q: Identify the Quakers and their core beliefs.
cards.a: The Quakers (Society of Friends) believed in an 'inner light' of God in every person. That led to spiritual equality of women and men, no ordained clergy, refusal to swear oaths or bow to social superiors, pacifism and, over time, opposition to slavery. Persecuted in England and in Massachusetts, which hanged four Quakers between 1659 and 1661, they made Pennsylvania a colony of religious toleration.
cards.h: → core belief + what followed from it + where they settled
cards.n: Quaker antislavery grew slowly from the 1688 Germantown protest, and many early Pennsylvania Quakers held slaves; 'always abolitionist' earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify William Penn and the founding of Pennsylvania.
cards.a: William Penn, a wealthy Quaker, received Pennsylvania from Charles II in 1681 as a proprietary colony, in payment of a royal debt owed to his father. He guaranteed religious toleration and an elected assembly, advertised for settlers across Britain and Europe, and bought land from the Lenape rather than simply seizing it. Philadelphia became the fastest-growing port in the colonies.
cards.h: → who + when + how he governed + result
cards.n: Penn's fair dealing did not last: his sons' Walking Purchase (1737) cheated the Lenape of their land. Toleration plus land made Pennsylvania the most diverse colony.

cards.q: Identify William Penn's 'Holy Experiment.'
cards.a: The 'Holy Experiment' was Penn's plan for Pennsylvania as a Quaker-led society that would prove toleration and peace could prosper: freedom of worship for all who believed in God, no established church, an elected assembly, milder laws, and purchase of land from the Lenape. It drew Quakers, Germans, Welsh and later Scots-Irish settlers and made the colony a model of pluralism.
cards.h: → Penn's aim + its main features + result
cards.n: This card asks for the plan's principles, not the founding story; 'a colony for Quakers only' misreads it.

cards.q: Identify the defining economic and social features of the Middle Colonies.
cards.a: The middle colonies (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware) exported wheat, flour and other cereal crops, earning the name 'breadbasket', and their family farms and tenant estates fed busy ports such as Philadelphia and New York. They drew the widest range of European migrants (Dutch, Germans, Scots-Irish, Swedes, Quakers, Jews) and practiced more religious toleration than New England or the South.
cards.h: → colonies + economy + population + religion
cards.n: Calling them a plantation region earns nothing, though their port cities held many enslaved people; their diversity is the standard contrast with Puritan New England.

cards.q: Identify the economy and labor system of South Carolina and the British Caribbean.
cards.a: South Carolina's lowcountry grew rice (and from the 1740s indigo), and Barbados and Jamaica grew sugar, on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Long growing seasons made these export crops profitable, and enslaved people became the majority of the population. West African knowledge of rice growing helped build the Carolina rice economy.
cards.h: → crops + labor + population + environment
cards.n: Black majorities produced both the harshest slave codes and the strongest survival of African culture, such as Gullah. How far rice relied on African expertise is debated.

cards.q: Explain the 'Barbados connection' in South Carolina's founding.
cards.a: Carolina, chartered in 1663 and settled at Charles Town from 1670, drew many early planters from Barbados, a crowded sugar island short of land. They brought the Caribbean model of large plantations, a Black-majority labor force and a harsh slave code (South Carolina's 1696 code drew on Barbados's 1661 code), so South Carolina came to resemble the West Indies more than Virginia.
cards.h: → who came from where + what they brought + result
cards.n: The point is the transfer of a whole system; 'some settlers came from Barbados' without what they brought earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify Eliza Lucas Pinckney and her development of indigo as a South Carolina cash crop.
cards.a: Eliza Lucas (later Pinckney), managing her father's South Carolina plantations as a teenager in the early 1740s, experimented with West Indian indigo seed until she produced a marketable dye, with hired indigo makers from the West Indies and the labor of enslaved workers. Indigo became South Carolina's second staple after rice, helped by a British bounty from 1748.
cards.h: → who + when + what she developed + its result
cards.n: Crediting her alone erases the enslaved labor and West Indian expertise behind the crop; indigo also depended on a British bounty, a mercantilist subsidy.

cards.q: Identify James Oglethorpe and the founding of Georgia.
cards.a: James Oglethorpe, a British soldier and philanthropist, led the founding of Georgia in 1733 under a board of trustees chartered in 1732. Georgia was meant as a buffer against Spanish Florida and as a fresh start for the 'worthy poor'; though debtor relief inspired it, few debtors actually went. It was the last of the thirteen colonies to be founded.
cards.h: → who + when + two purposes
cards.n: The debtor-haven story is overstated: few debtors came. Defense against Spanish Florida was the purpose London cared about.

cards.q: Explain how tobacco saved and shaped the Virginia colony.
cards.a: Tobacco gave Virginia its first profitable export. After John Rolfe grew a milder West Indian strain from 1612, planters grew it everywhere; its labor demands drew indentured servants and then enslaved Africans, and its soil-draining fields pushed settlement onto Powhatan land.
cards.h: → Rolfe's strain → profitable export → labor demand (servants, then slaves) + land hunger → conflict with the Powhatan
cards.n: 'Tobacco made Virginia rich' is a claim with no mechanism; the point is how one crop drove the labor system and land conflict.
o: Tobacco turned a failing company outpost into a colony worth settling: by 1617 Virginians were planting it even in Jamestown's streets.
Because tobacco paid, the headright system rewarded planters who imported laborers, so the crop shaped both landholding and the labor force.

w.a: Tobacco saved Virginia because colonists smoked it to stay healthy.
w.why: misreads the crop's role; it mattered as an export

w.a: Tobacco saved Virginia by making peace with the Powhatan possible.
w.why: backwards; tobacco's land hunger fed conflict, as in 1622

w.a: Tobacco mattered because slaves grew it from the start.
w.why: false; servants did most of the work until about 1680

cards.q: Explain how tobacco monoculture affected Chesapeake soil and settlement patterns.
cards.a: Tobacco drained soil nutrients within a few years, and planters with much land and scarce labor abandoned worn fields rather than manure them. So they kept clearing new ground, spread along rivers in scattered plantations rather than towns, and pressed inland onto Native land.
cards.h: → tobacco exhausts soil → planters clear new fields → scattered riverside plantations, few towns → push onto Native land
cards.n: Stopping at 'tobacco ruined the soil' earns nothing; the point is the effect on settlement: dispersal, few towns and westward land hunger.
o: Because ships could load tobacco at each planter's riverside wharf, the Chesapeake needed few towns or ports, unlike New England.
Soil exhaustion helps explain why freed servants of the 1670s found little good land near the coast, one root of Bacon's Rebellion.

w.a: Tobacco monoculture made Chesapeake soil more fertile over time.
w.why: false; tobacco depleted soil quickly

w.a: Tobacco made colonists settle in tight towns like New England's.
w.why: backwards; Chesapeake settlement was dispersed

w.a: Worn-out soil made planters switch to wheat right away.
w.why: overstated; the shift to wheat came gradually, mostly after 1750

cards.q: Explain why New England developed a mixed economy of farming and commerce rather than a plantation economy.
cards.a: Its environment ruled out a cash staple: thin, rocky soil and a short growing season suited small family farms, not tobacco or rice. So New Englanders added fishing, lumbering, shipbuilding and trade, sending fish and timber to the West Indies, and needed few bound laborers.
cards.h: → rocky soil + short season → no cash staple → family farms + fish, timber, ships, trade → little need for bound labor
cards.n: Saying Puritans simply rejected slavery earns nothing; New Englanders held and traded slaves. Environment and farm size explain the economy.
o: Family migration gave New England many hands for small farms, so it never faced the Chesapeake's hunger for imported labor.
Good harbors and forests made shipbuilding and Atlantic trade the region's route to wealth, linking it to the plantation colonies it supplied.

w.a: New England had a mixed economy because Puritans thought farming was sinful.
w.why: false; most New Englanders were farmers

w.a: New England had no plantations because slavery was illegal there.
w.why: false; Massachusetts legalized slavery in 1641

w.a: New England traded because it had no farmland at all.
w.why: overstated; family farms were the base of its economy

cards.q: Explain why New England's population grew mainly by natural increase while the early Chesapeake's depended on immigration.
cards.a: New Englanders came as families to a cool, healthy climate, so balanced sex ratios and long lives made large families. Early Chesapeake migrants were mostly young single men, and malaria, typhoid and dysentery in the tidewater killed many, so the region grew by importing people until about 1700.
cards.h: → families + healthy climate → many births, long lives vs single men + disease → high deaths → growth by import
cards.n: Naming only religion as the difference earns nothing; the demographic contrast rests on sex ratios and the disease environment.
o: Men who survived childhood lived to about 70 in New England but only to the mid-40s in the early Chesapeake (estimates), so New England families were far larger.
Men outnumbered women several to one among early Chesapeake migrants, so few families formed until native-born colonists came of age around 1700.

w.a: New England grew faster because Puritans kept arriving after 1640.
w.why: false; migration nearly stopped in the early 1640s

w.a: The Chesapeake grew slowly because planters did not want children.
w.why: no mechanism; sex ratios and disease explain it

w.a: Both regions grew the same way, by immigration.
w.why: ignores the contrast the question asks about

cards.q: Explain why colonial self-governing institutions were unusually democratic for the era.
cards.a: Distance and Britain's lax attention left colonists to run their own affairs, and charters and English law gave them a claim to elected assemblies. Because land was cheap and widely owned, a far larger share of white men (by most estimates a majority) met the property test to vote than in England.
cards.h: → distance + neglect → colonists govern themselves; cheap land → many freeholders → wide white male suffrage
cards.n: 'Everyone could vote' is false and earns nothing; women, the enslaved and the propertyless were excluded. The claim is 'unusually democratic for the era'.
o: New England town meetings let ordinary male householders debate and vote on local taxes, schools and roads, a practice rare in Europe.
New France and New Spain had no elected assemblies at all, so the British colonies stood out among the empires in America.

w.a: The colonies were democratic because Britain wanted to spread democracy.
w.why: misreads British aims; autonomy came from neglect

w.a: Colonial governments were democratic because all adults could vote.
w.why: false; voting was limited to free white men, mostly with property

w.a: Self-government was democratic because the colonies had no governors.
w.why: false; most had royal or proprietary governors

cards.q: Explain why the middle colonies were more ethnically and religiously diverse than New England.
cards.a: The middle colonies began mixed and chose toleration: New York inherited a varied Dutch trading population, and Quaker Pennsylvania welcomed all Christians. Rich grain land and open ports then drew Germans and Scots-Irish. Puritan New England, founded as one covenanted community, discouraged outsiders.
cards.h: → Dutch mixed origins + Quaker toleration + good land and ports → varied migrants; Puritan uniformity → few outsiders
cards.n: 'The middle colonies were more tolerant' restates the question; name the founding origins and the economic pull that produced diversity.
o: Proprietors in Pennsylvania and New Jersey needed settlers to make their grants pay, so they recruited widely and promised freedom of worship.
New England towns granted land to covenanted church communities, which kept strangers out and preserved ethnic and religious uniformity.

w.a: The middle colonies were diverse because the Spanish founded them.
w.why: false; Dutch, Swedish and English founders

w.a: New England was less diverse because ships could not reach it.
w.why: false; Boston was a major port

w.a: The middle colonies were diverse because they held the most slaves.
w.why: false; the lowcountry held far more

cards.q: Define mercantilism.
cards.a: Mercantilism was the economic theory that a nation grows powerful by exporting more than it imports and accumulating gold and silver, on the assumption that the world's wealth is limited. Colonies existed to supply the mother country with raw materials and to buy its manufactured goods, and trade laws kept those profits inside the empire.
cards.h: → the theory + the colonies' role + how it was enforced
cards.n: Equating mercantilism with free trade, or with taxes meant to raise revenue, earns nothing; its laws aimed to keep the empire's commerce in British hands.

cards.q: Identify the Navigation Acts.
cards.a: The Navigation Acts, English laws of 1651, 1660, 1663 and 1696, required colonial trade to travel in English or colonial ships, required 'enumerated' goods such as tobacco, sugar and later rice to be shipped only to England or other English colonies, and routed most European imports through England. The 1696 act added customs officers and vice-admiralty courts to enforce them.
cards.h: → years + three main rules + enforcement
cards.n: They were enforced only loosely before 1763, and strict enforcement afterward is what felt new. Calling them taxes to raise revenue misreads their purpose.

cards.q: Explain both the costs and the benefits of the Navigation Acts for the colonies.
cards.a: Costs: colonists could sell enumerated goods such as tobacco only through England, paid more for European imports routed through England, and faced limits on manufacturing. Benefits: a protected British market for their staples, bounties on goods such as indigo and naval stores, a booming colonial shipbuilding industry (colonial ships counted as English), and the Royal Navy's protection. Widespread smuggling softened the costs further.
cards.h: → costs, then benefits, then how enforcement shaped them
cards.n: A one-sided answer misses the balance the question asks for; claiming the Acts alone caused the Revolution skips everything from 1763 to 1776.

cards.q: Identify the Wool, Hat, and Iron Acts and the mercantilist aim behind them.
cards.a: The Wool Act (1699) barred colonists from exporting wool and woolen cloth; the Hat Act (1732) banned exporting colonial hats, even to other colonies; and the Iron Act (1750) let colonial pig and bar iron into Britain duty-free but forbade new colonial mills for finishing iron. Each protected British manufacturers, so the colonies would supply raw materials and buy finished goods.
cards.h: → each act + year + what it limited + the aim
cards.n: 'Britain banned all colonial manufacturing' overstates them; weakly enforced, they mattered more as grievances than as barriers.

cards.q: Identify the Board of Trade of 1696 and the vice-admiralty courts, and what they were meant to do.
cards.a: In 1696 the crown created the Board of Trade (the Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations) to oversee colonial commerce and review colonial laws, and that year's Navigation Act set up vice-admiralty courts in the colonies to try smuggling cases without juries. Both aimed to fold the colonies into a coherent imperial system; understaffing and colonial resistance made enforcement erratic.
cards.h: → year + each body's job + how well it worked
cards.n: Britain revived this 1690s machinery after 1763, when jury-less admiralty courts became a grievance; before then its weak record is the CED's 'erratic enforcement'.

cards.q: Define salutary neglect.
cards.a: Salutary neglect was Britain's informal practice, from about the 1690s to 1763 and especially under Prime Minister Robert Walpole (1721-1742), of loosely enforcing its trade laws and leaving colonial assemblies to run their own affairs. Britain reasoned that prosperous, lightly governed colonies enriched the empire more than strict control would.
cards.h: → what it was + when + why Britain allowed it
cards.n: It was a practice, never a law; the name comes from Edmund Burke's 1775 speech. It is the 'erratic enforcement' the CED describes.

cards.q: Identify the Dominion of New England and Sir Edmund Andros.
cards.a: The Dominion of New England (1686-1689) was James II's merger of the New England colonies, later joined by New York and New Jersey, into one royal province under Governor Sir Edmund Andros. Andros ruled without an elected assembly, challenged land titles, restricted town meetings and enforced the Navigation Acts, provoking deep resentment. It collapsed when Bostonians overthrew him in 1689.
cards.h: → when + what it combined + what Andros did + its end
cards.n: It is the CED's 'coherent, hierarchical, and imperial structure' in action, and its collapse shows enforcement's limits; colonists recalled it in the 1760s.

cards.q: Define the Molasses Act of 1733.
cards.a: The Molasses Act of 1733 put a duty of sixpence a gallon on molasses imported into the mainland colonies from foreign, chiefly French, West Indian islands, to protect British sugar planters. New England rum distillers relied on cheaper French molasses, so merchants evaded the duty by smuggling and bribery, and it raised little revenue.
cards.h: → year + what it taxed + whom it protected + result
cards.n: Its evasion shows the erratic enforcement; the Sugar Act of 1764 cut the duty to threepence but enforced it, and that is what angered colonists.

cards.q: Explain the economic importance of naval stores production in colonial North Carolina.
cards.a: North Carolina's longleaf pine forests yielded tar, pitch and turpentine, which the Royal Navy needed to seal and preserve wooden ships and rigging. Parliament's Naval Stores Act of 1705 paid bounties for colonial naval stores to end dependence on Swedish (Baltic) supplies, and North Carolina became the empire's leading producer, often with enslaved labor. It shows mercantilism steering a colonial economy.
cards.h: → products + why Britain wanted them + policy + result
cards.n: Naming the products without the imperial motive, bounties to escape reliance on Swedish supplies, misses the mercantilist point.

cards.q: Define the triangular trade.
cards.a: The triangular trade is a simplified model of Atlantic commerce: New England rum and manufactured goods went to West Africa; enslaved Africans were carried to the West Indies and the mainland colonies; and sugar and molasses returned to New England to be distilled into rum, while staples went to Britain. Real routes were many and messier, but the model ties the northern colonies' economy to slavery.
cards.h: → three legs + goods on each + a caveat
cards.n: Treating it as one fixed three-stop route loses nuance, since most voyages shuttled between two points; the scored idea is the North's economic tie to slavery.

cards.q: Define the Middle Passage.
cards.a: The Middle Passage was the forced Atlantic crossing of enslaved Africans from West and West-Central Africa to the Americas, the middle leg of the Atlantic trade. Captives were chained below decks for weeks to months in crowded, disease-ridden holds; about 12.5 million people were embarked over the trade's history, and roughly one in seven died at sea.
cards.h: → what it was + conditions + scale
cards.n: Figures are Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database estimates. Only about 400,000 captives landed in mainland North America; most went to Brazil and the Caribbean.

cards.q: Identify the trade in enslaved American Indians centered on Charles Town, South Carolina.
cards.a: From the 1670s to about 1715 Carolina traders bought Native captives taken in raids by allied nations, first the Westo and later the Yamasee and Creek, and shipped many to the West Indies or sold them locally. Historians estimate that roughly 24,000 to 51,000 Native people in the Southeast were enslaved this way. The raids devastated Spanish Florida's missions and helped provoke the Yamasee War of 1715.
cards.h: → when + how it worked + scale + consequence
cards.n: KC-2.1.III.A names enslaved American Indians beside Africans in the Atlantic economy; leaving them out misses that. The totals are estimates (Alan Gallay).

cards.q: Describe how trade with Europeans changed American Indian communities in the 1600s and 1700s.
cards.a: Trade brought metal tools, kettles, guns, cloth and alcohol into Native villages, which made hunting and warfare deadlier and daily work easier but bred dependence on European goods and credit. To pay, men hunted beaver and deer far beyond their own needs, depleting the animals and pushing nations to fight over hunting grounds. Trade contacts also spread epidemics such as smallpox that caused radical population loss.
cards.h: → goods in + what Natives did to pay + disease
cards.n: One-way exploitation misses Native choice: nations sought trade and bargained hard. But dependence and epidemics followed, as KC-2.1.III.B says.

cards.q: Identify the main origin and destination of each commodity in the eighteenth-century Atlantic economy: tobacco · rice · indigo · sugar and molasses · rum · dried cod · wheat and flour · furs · deerskins · naval stores · enslaved Africans · British cloth and hardware
cards.a:
tobacco → Chesapeake to Britain (enumerated; much re-exported to Europe)
rice → South Carolina lowcountry to Britain and southern Europe (enumerated from 1704)
indigo → South Carolina to Britain (bounty from 1748)
sugar and molasses → British and French West Indies to Britain (sugar) and New England (molasses)
rum → New England distilleries to Africa, the fisheries and other colonies
dried cod → New England to the West Indies (low grades, to feed enslaved people) and southern Europe (best grades)
wheat and flour → middle colonies to the West Indies and southern Europe
furs → Native hunters via New France, Albany and Hudson Bay to Europe
deerskins → southeastern Native hunters via Charles Town to Britain
naval stores → North Carolina to Britain (bounties from 1705)
enslaved Africans → West and West-Central Africa to the Caribbean and Brazil above all, and to the mainland colonies
British cloth and hardware → Britain to every colony and, through traders, to Native nations and African markets
cards.h: → from where → to where, each commodity
cards.n: Sending most enslaved Africans to the mainland colonies is the classic error; the great majority went to the Caribbean and Brazil.

cards.q: Explain how the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 affected the American colonies.
cards.a: It toppled the imperial overreach the colonies had just suffered. When news of James II's fall arrived in 1689, Bostonians jailed Andros and the Dominion collapsed; Leisler seized New York and Protestants rose in Maryland. The new monarchs allowed assemblies again, though Massachusetts got a royal governor in 1691.
cards.h: → James II falls → colonists topple Andros and the Dominion → risings in New York, Maryland → assemblies restored
cards.n: Saying the colonies broke from the king in 1689 earns nothing; colonists acted as loyal Englishmen defending English rights.
o: The Glorious Revolution's settlement, including the 1689 Bill of Rights and Locke's defense of it, gave colonists a model of subjects checking a king.
It ended the attempt to rule without assemblies, so later imperial reform worked through royal governors and the Board of Trade instead.

w.a: The Glorious Revolution made the colonies independent from Britain.
w.why: false; they remained loyal colonies

w.a: The Glorious Revolution had no effect because it happened in England.
w.why: ignores the Boston, New York and Maryland risings

w.a: The Glorious Revolution created the Dominion of New England.
w.why: backwards; it destroyed the Dominion

cards.q: Explain why Britain enforced its imperial trade laws only erratically before 1754.
cards.a: Enforcement cost more than it seemed worth. Customs officers were few, underpaid and easily bribed along a long coast; ministers such as Walpole judged that thriving colonies already enriched Britain; and assemblies that paid officials could stall royal governors. Wars with France made goodwill valuable too.
cards.h: → few, bribable officials + profitable trade anyway + assemblies hold the purse + wartime needs → lax enforcement
cards.n: Saying Britain 'did not care' about the colonies earns nothing; Britain cared about the trade and chose leniency because it paid.
o: Conflict with colonists, as when Boston overthrew the Dominion in 1689, showed ministers that tight control could provoke revolt.
Smuggling French molasses was so profitable, and so tolerated by local juries, that the Molasses Act raised almost nothing.

w.a: Britain did not enforce its laws because it had no navy.
w.why: false; it had the largest navy in the world

w.a: Britain enforced its laws strictly, which is why colonists smuggled.
w.why: contradicts the premise; lax enforcement made smuggling easy

w.a: Britain did not care what happened in the colonies.
w.why: false; it passed trade laws and fought wars over them

cards.q: Explain why the Navigation Acts both tied the colonies to Britain and fed colonial resentment.
cards.a: The Acts gave colonists protected markets, bounties and Royal Navy protection, and colonial-built ships counted as English, so trade with Britain boomed. But they capped colonial prices and manufacturing and, when enforced as under the Dominion, overrode assemblies, so colonists learned to evade and resent them.
cards.h: → protected market + bounties + navy → closer trade ties; price limits + bursts of enforcement → evasion, resentment
cards.n: Arguing only resentment or only benefit misses KC-2.2's point that the same exchanges both bound and chafed.
o: Because enforcement was lax, most colonists felt the benefits more than the costs before 1763, which is why strict enforcement afterward shocked them.
Chesapeake planters resented selling tobacco only through England at low prices, yet depended on British credit and markets to sell it at all.

w.a: The Navigation Acts only hurt the colonies.
w.why: ignores protected markets, bounties and shipbuilding

w.a: Colonists resented the Acts because they included the Stamp Act.
w.why: conflates periods; the Stamp Act came in 1765

w.a: The Acts tied the colonies to Britain by taxing colonists directly.
w.why: false; they regulated trade, not direct taxes

cards.q: Explain why New England merchants depended on trade with the West Indies.
cards.a: The sugar islands grew little food because nearly every acre went to cane, so they bought New England's fish, timber, barrel staves and livestock. Merchants took molasses in return, distilled it into rum, and earned credit to pay for British goods. The islands let New England earn what its soil could not.
cards.h: → sugar islands grow little food → buy fish, timber, livestock → molasses and credit return → rum + British imports
cards.n: Missing the plantation link loses the point: New England's commercial prosperity rested on feeding and supplying slave societies.
o: Low-grade dried cod was sold in the West Indies as cheap food for enslaved workers, tying New England's fisheries directly to plantation slavery.
New England produced no staple Britain wanted, so selling to the islands was how it paid for British imports.

w.a: New England traded with the West Indies because it grew sugar there.
w.why: New England grew no sugar; it bought molasses

w.a: New England traded there because the Navigation Acts required it.
w.why: the Acts did not require it; the market did

w.a: New England traded with the West Indies to end slavery there.
w.why: false; the trade sustained slavery

cards.q: Explain why the fur and deerskin trades led to warfare among American Indian nations.
cards.a: European goods, above all guns and metal tools, became necessities that nations paid for in pelts. As hunting stripped beaver and deer near home, nations fought for new hunting grounds and for control of trade with Europeans, as in the Iroquois wars on the Huron in the 1640s; guns made those wars deadlier.
cards.h: → dependence on trade goods → overhunting → fights over hunting grounds and trade routes → deadlier armed wars
cards.n: 'Europeans made the Natives fight' removes Native agency; nations fought for their own economic and political goals, with European weapons.
o: Epidemics spread along trade routes, and some nations raided rivals for captives to replace their dead, a mourning-war pattern the fur trade intensified.
Middleman positions, such as the Huron's between the French and interior nations, were so profitable that rivals tried to break them by force.

w.a: Native nations fought because they had never fought before trade.
w.why: false; Native warfare long predated contact

w.a: The fur trade brought peace because everyone profited.
w.why: ignores the Beaver Wars and deerskin-trade conflicts

w.a: The wars happened because Europeans ordered Native nations to fight.
w.why: denies Native agency and names no economic cause

cards.q: Identify the Powhatan paramount chiefdom and how it first dealt with Jamestown.
cards.a: Wahunsenacawh, called Powhatan by the English, ruled a paramount chiefdom of some thirty Algonquian-speaking peoples in tidewater Virginia. He first tried to absorb the English as useful, subordinate trading partners, exchanging corn for metal goods and withholding food when colonists grew demanding. The capture of his daughter Pocahontas and her 1614 marriage to John Rolfe brought an uneasy peace that lasted until 1622.
cards.h: → who + his strategy toward the English + the 1614 peace
cards.n: The Pocahontas romance myth earns nothing; her marriage followed her capture as a hostage in 1613 and worked as diplomacy.

cards.q: Identify Opechancanough's 1622 uprising against Jamestown.
cards.a: On March 22, 1622, Opechancanough, Wahunsenacawh's brother and successor, launched coordinated surprise attacks on English settlements along the James River that killed about 347 colonists, roughly a quarter of Virginia's English population. The English answered with years of raids destroying Powhatan towns and crops, ending hopes of coexistence, and the disaster helped lead the crown to revoke the Virginia Company's charter in 1624.
cards.h: → who + when + what happened + the English response
cards.n: Blaming 'Native treachery' without the cause, English expansion onto Powhatan land for tobacco, earns nothing. Opechancanough struck again in 1644.

cards.q: Identify Tisquantum (Squanto) and his role in the Plymouth colony's survival.
cards.a: Tisquantum (Squanto) was a Patuxet man kidnapped by an English captain in 1614 and sold in Spain; he reached England and returned home in 1619 to find his people wiped out by epidemic. In 1621 he interpreted between the Plymouth Pilgrims and the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit, taught the colonists to plant corn with fish as fertilizer, and helped seal the alliance that kept the colony alive.
cards.h: → who + his past + what he did for Plymouth
cards.n: Massasoit allied with Plymouth for his own reasons, protection from the Narragansett after epidemics; the 1621 feast was diplomacy, not the 1863 national holiday.

cards.q: Identify the Pequot War.
cards.a: The Pequot War (1636-1637) pitted Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut colonists, allied with the Narragansett and Mohegan, against the Pequot, who dominated trade in southern New England. In May 1637 the English and their allies burned the fortified Pequot village at Mystic, killing some 400 to 700 people, mostly women, children and old men. The war destroyed the Pequot as a nation and opened the Connecticut valley to English settlement.
cards.h: → when + who fought whom + key event + result
cards.n: It shows the English using Native allies against a Native rival (KC-2.1.III.C); the Narragansett, shocked at Mystic, judged English warfare too brutal.

cards.q: Identify King Philip's War (Metacom's War).
cards.a: King Philip's War (1675-1676), or Metacom's War, was an uprising led by Metacom, the Wampanoag sachem the English called King Philip, joined by the Nipmuc and, after an English attack in December 1675, the Narragansett, against expanding New England settlement. More than half of New England's roughly 90 towns were attacked and about a dozen destroyed; Native losses to death, flight and sale into slavery were far worse. It ended Native military power in southern New England.
cards.h: → when + leader + who joined + scale + result
cards.n: Pairs with Bacon's Rebellion in the same years as the 1670s land crises. 'Proportionally the deadliest war in American history' is a historians' estimate.

cards.q: Contrast the Pequot War and King Philip's War in scale and consequence.
cards.a: The Pequot War (1636-1637) was a short war against a single nation early in settlement, won with Narragansett and Mohegan allies, and it opened the Connecticut valley. King Philip's War (1675-1676) came four decades later, after English numbers and land hunger had grown; it was a multi-nation coalition war, far bloodier for both sides, and it permanently ended Native military resistance in southern New England.
cards.h: → scale + who fought + consequence of each
cards.n: The continuity is English land pressure; the change is Native strategy, from one nation to a coalition. Two lists of facts with no stated difference earn nothing.

cards.q: Identify Bacon's Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1676 Nathaniel Bacon, a wealthy newcomer, led frontier farmers, former indentured servants and some enslaved and free Black Virginians first against Native peoples, including friendly ones, and then against Governor William Berkeley, who had refused to wage all-out war on Native nations to open more land. The rebels burned Jamestown; the rising collapsed after Bacon died of dysentery in October 1676.
cards.h: → year + who + against whom + why + how it ended
cards.n: It began as a war on Native peoples (KC-2.1.III.E) and grew into a revolt of the landless poor; missing the land-and-frontier cause loses the point.

cards.q: Identify the Beaver Wars and the European alliances behind them.
cards.a: The Beaver Wars were conflicts from the 1640s to 1701 in which the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee), armed with Dutch and later English guns, fought the Huron (Wendat) and other French-allied nations for furs, hunting grounds and captives. The Iroquois destroyed the Huron confederacy in 1649 and drove other peoples west, and the wars ended with the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701.
cards.h: → when + who fought whom + who armed each side + outcome
cards.n: The name is a historians' label and not only about beaver: taking captives to replace epidemic losses drove the wars too. It is KC-2.1.III.C's armed alliances in action.

cards.q: Identify the Covenant Chain linking the Iroquois Confederacy to the English colonies.
cards.a: The Covenant Chain was a set of alliances, formalized at Albany from 1677, linking the Iroquois Confederacy with New York and, through it, other English colonies. It coordinated trade and diplomacy, let the Iroquois claim to speak for other Native nations in dealings with the English, and made New York their main European partner. After 1701 the Iroquois balanced it with peace and neutrality toward France.
cards.h: → when + whom it linked + what it did for each side
cards.n: Treating the Iroquois as English puppets misreads it; the Covenant Chain was a tool of Iroquois diplomacy, played against French ties after 1701.

cards.q: Define the 'middle ground' as historians use the term for the Great Lakes region.
cards.a: Historian Richard White's term for the Great Lakes region (the pays d'en haut) from about 1650 to 1815, where neither the French nor the Algonquian nations could dominate the other, so both accommodated: they exchanged gifts, mediated disputes, intermarried and built shared customs, often by creatively misreading each other's ways. It names accommodation born of mutual need, which broke down once one side, the British and later the Americans, could impose its will.
cards.h: → whose term + where and when + what it describes + its end
cards.n: Using 'middle ground' for any friendly relationship earns nothing; it names mutual dependence, where neither side could force the other.

cards.q: Identify the Tuscarora War of 1711-1715 and its long-term result for the Iroquois Confederacy.
cards.a: The Tuscarora War (1711-1715) began when the Tuscarora of North Carolina, angered by settler encroachment, trader abuses and the enslaving of their people, attacked colonial settlements; South Carolina forces and their Yamasee and other Native allies crushed them. Many survivors moved north and were adopted into the Iroquois Confederacy around 1722, which became the Six Nations.
cards.h: → when + causes + outcome + the Iroquois link
cards.n: The Yamasee War (1715) followed at once; both grew out of trader abuses and the southern trade in enslaved Native people.

cards.q: Identify the Yamasee War and its causes.
cards.a: In 1715 the Yamasee, joined by Creeks, Catawbas and others, attacked South Carolina over traders' abuses, debts that traders collected by seizing Native people as slaves, and encroachment on their land. The war killed hundreds of colonists and nearly destroyed the colony until Cherokee help turned it in 1716. It gutted the Carolina trade in enslaved Native people, and South Carolina leaned even harder on enslaved Africans.
cards.h: → when + who + causes + outcome
cards.n: It links 2.4 and 2.5: the deerskin and Indian slave trades bred the debts and abuses behind it. Casualty figures are estimates.

cards.q: Describe how Spanish policy toward the Pueblos changed after the reconquest of New Mexico in the 1690s.
cards.a: After Diego de Vargas retook New Mexico (1692-1696), Spain ruled more by accommodation. The encomienda's forced tribute was not restored, friars tolerated more Pueblo ceremonies alongside Catholic worship, Pueblo towns kept their lands under Spanish grants, and Spaniards and Pueblos fought together against Apache, Navajo and Comanche raiders. Spanish rule remained, but on terms worked out with Pueblo communities.
cards.h: → who retook it + four changes + the overall shift
cards.n: Saying Spain simply crushed the Pueblos again earns nothing; KC-2.1.III.F is about accommodation. The 1680 revolt itself is carded in u1.

cards.q: Identify the point of view and historical situation of this source, and one limitation they create. (Paraphrase written for this deck of the December 1681 declaration of Pedro Naranjo, a Keres Pueblo man captured by Spanish forces and questioned through an interpreter: the leader Popé had ordered the people to burn the churches and holy images, to stop speaking Spanish, to wash away their baptisms in the rivers, and to return to the ways of their ancestors, promising that they would then live in health and plenty.)
cards.a: Point of view: a Pueblo participant explaining the revolt's aims, but as a prisoner answering Spanish questions. Situation: Governor Otermin's failed attempt (1681-1682) to retake New Mexico a year after the 1680 revolt drove the Spanish out. Limitation: a captive speaking through an interpreter to his enemies may have shaded his account, and Spanish scribes chose what to record, so it may overstate Popé's control or the revolt's anti-Christian aims.
cards.h: → point of view + situation + how they limit the source
cards.n: Identifying the speaker ('a Pueblo man') without explaining how capture and translation shape what he said earns nothing on a sourcing task.

cards.q: Identify the purpose and intended audience of Mary Rowlandson's captivity narrative (1682), and explain how they limit it as evidence about Native peoples in King Philip's War.
cards.a: Rowlandson, a minister's wife captured in the February 1676 raid on Lancaster, Massachusetts, and ransomed after about eleven weeks, wrote for a Puritan readership to show God's providence in her suffering and redemption. Because she cast her captors as instruments of divine testing and called them 'barbarous' and 'heathen', the narrative says more about Puritan belief than about Native motives, though it records her captors' hunger and her dealings with Metacom in detail.
cards.h: → purpose + audience + how they limit the source
cards.n: 'She is biased because she was captured' is too vague to earn the point; name the purpose (a Puritan providence tale) and show how it shapes what she reports.

cards.q: Identify the point of view of this source and explain its significance. (Paraphrase written for this deck of John Easton's report of a June 1675 meeting with Metacom, written by Rhode Island's deputy governor: Metacom complained that the English cheated his people of land through deeds signed by drunken sachems, let their cattle and horses trample Native cornfields, sold his people liquor, and judged them in English courts where Native testimony counted for nothing.)
cards.a: Point of view: Metacom's grievances as reported by John Easton, a Quaker deputy governor of Rhode Island who hoped to prevent war and had little love for Plymouth. Significance: written before the fighting by a sympathetic outsider, it is one of the few sources giving Native causes of King Philip's War (land loss, livestock, English courts), though it still reaches us through an English author.
cards.h: → whose view + through whom + why it matters + a limit
cards.n: Treating the grievances as Metacom's own words loses the sourcing point: an English Quaker recorded them, with his own reasons to blame Plymouth.

cards.q: Explain why French relations with American Indians were generally less violent than English relations with them.
cards.a: France wanted furs and allies; England wanted land. Few French colonists farmed, so French traders and priests lived among Native nations, gave gifts and intermarried. English farm families multiplied and took land, which led to wars such as the Pequot War and King Philip's War.
cards.h: → French: furs, few settlers → gifts, alliance, intermarriage; English: families take land → wars
cards.n: 'The French were nicer' earns nothing; French wars on the Iroquois, Fox and Natchez show the difference lay in economic need, not temperament.
o: Native nations valued the French alliance because France threatened their land far less, which is why most sided with France in 1754.
Where France did want land, as at Natchez in 1729, the French fought and enslaved Native people much as the English did.

w.a: The French were less violent because they converted all Native people.
w.why: false; conversions were limited and explain nothing

w.a: The French never fought any Native nation.
w.why: false; they fought the Iroquois, Fox and Natchez

w.a: The English fought more because they had more guns.
w.why: no mechanism; land hunger drove the conflicts

cards.q: Explain why Spain accommodated aspects of Pueblo culture after the Pueblo Revolt.
cards.a: The 1680 revolt showed Spain that rule by force and forced labor could cost it the colony. After retaking New Mexico it needed Pueblo cooperation to survive Apache and Comanche raids, so it dropped the encomienda's tribute, tolerated some Pueblo rites and made the Pueblos military allies.
cards.h: → 1680 revolt expels Spain → costly lesson → need for Pueblo allies against raiders → accommodation
cards.n: Stating the accommodation without its causes, the revolt's lesson and the raiding threat, describes rather than explains.
o: A thinly settled colony far from Mexico City could not hold down a hostile majority, so compromise was cheaper than conquest.
Mounted Apache and later Comanche raiders threatened Spaniards and Pueblos alike, giving both a shared enemy.

w.a: Spain accommodated the Pueblos because it came to respect their religion.
w.why: sentiment; the cause was the revolt's cost and the need for allies

w.a: Spain accommodated the Pueblos because it lost New Mexico forever in 1680.
w.why: false; Spain retook it in 1692

w.a: Spain accommodated the Pueblos because the Pope ordered it.
w.why: invented; no pope ordered it (Popé led the revolt)

cards.q: Explain why American Indian nations sought alliances with European powers against other Native nations.
cards.a: Alliances served Native goals. A European partner supplied guns, metal tools and trade that gave an edge over rivals, at a time when epidemics and war left every nation vulnerable. So the Iroquois, armed with Dutch guns, crushed the Huron, and the Mohegan and Narragansett joined the English against the Pequot.
cards.h: → Native rivalries + epidemics → need for guns and trade → European ally → edge over Native rivals
cards.n: Treating Native allies as European tools removes their agency; the exam wants the Native motive, advantage against Native rivals.
o: Nations caught between empires, such as the Iroquois after 1701, used alliances to extract gifts and keep their independence.
Massasoit allied with Plymouth in 1621 because epidemics had left the Wampanoag exposed to the stronger Narragansett.
