States also set voting qualifications, which usually required property.
cards.h: → which offices were filtered + how, one by one
cards.n: Calling the 1787 Constitution fully democratic misses its design: the framers deliberately filtered popular majorities while resting power on the people.

cards.q: Identify how the original Constitution provided for choosing the president and vice president.
cards.a: Each state chose electors, equal to its number of representatives plus senators, in whatever way its legislature directed. Each elector cast two votes for president; the candidate with the most votes, if a majority of electors, became president and the runner-up vice president. With no majority or a tie, the House chose, each state delegation casting one vote. The Twelfth Amendment (1804) later required separate votes for the two offices.
cards.h: → electors + two votes + runner-up rule + House backup
cards.n: Assuming voters chose the president directly misreads 1787; the runner-up rule is what produced the split result of 1796 and the tie of 1800.

cards.q: Identify two features of the national government that continued from the Articles of Confederation into the Constitution, and the main change.
cards.a: Continuities: the national government kept the powers Congress had held under the Articles to make war and peace, coin and borrow money, run the post office and govern western territory, and the Northwest Ordinance was re-enacted in 1789; the states kept broad control of their internal affairs, such as property law and voting qualifications. The main change was new national power to tax, regulate commerce and enforce laws through a president and courts.
cards.h: → two continuities + the change
cards.n: Treating 1787 as a total break misses the question: name powers the Articles already granted that carried over, then the change.

cards.q: Explain why the Constitution created a central government that was both limited and dynamic.
cards.a: The framers wanted enough power to fix the Articles' failures but feared tyranny. So they listed Congress's powers and divided and checked authority, making it limited, yet granted taxing and commerce powers and a necessary and proper clause that let it stretch to new needs, making it dynamic.
cards.h: → Articles too weak + fear of tyranny → listed, divided, checked powers + tax, commerce, elastic clause
cards.n: Defining 'limited' and 'dynamic' without naming the provisions that make the government each earns little.
o: An amendment process easier than the Articles' unanimity let the Constitution change over time without a new convention.
Federalism left states strong in their own sphere while making national law supreme where it applied, a balance later generations kept renegotiating.

w.a: The Constitution was dynamic because the president could change it by decree.
w.why: false; amendment needs Congress and the states

w.a: The Constitution was limited because Congress still could not tax, as under the Articles.
w.why: reversed; the Constitution gave Congress taxing power

cards.q: Explain why the framers divided power between the national government and the states instead of abolishing the states.
cards.a: The states were existing political communities with their own constitutions and citizens' loyalty, and ratification needed their consent. Federalism gave the nation power over common concerns such as taxes, trade and defense, left local affairs to the states, and added another check on tyranny.
cards.h: → states already sovereign, needed to ratify → divide power → nation for common matters, states local, extra check
cards.n: 'To balance power' is a phrase; the answer needs the states' existing sovereignty and what each level controlled.
o: Madison argued in Federalist No. 51 that dividing power between two levels gave a 'double security' to the rights of the people.
Small states and slaveholding states would not accept a union that erased state power, so federalism was also a condition of agreement.

w.a: The framers kept the states because the Articles had already made them weak and harmless.
w.why: reversed; the Articles left the states powerful

w.a: Federalism means the national government is always subordinate to the states.
w.why: wrong; national law is supreme within its sphere

cards.q: Explain why the Constitution changed the national government's relationship with individual citizens compared with the Articles.
cards.a: Under the Articles, Congress acted only on the states, requesting money and troops they could refuse. The Constitution let the national government tax, make laws for and try individuals directly, through its own officers and courts, so its laws no longer depended on state cooperation.
cards.h: → Articles act on states, which refuse → Constitution acts on individuals → enforceable national law
cards.n: Saying the new government was 'stronger' without showing that it now reached individuals directly misses the change.
o: The supremacy clause made the Constitution, federal laws and treaties the supreme law, binding on state judges, which the Articles never achieved.
Because voters elected the House directly, the national government drew authority from the people, not only from the states.

w.a: Nothing changed, because the Constitution kept the Articles' system of requisitions.
w.why: false; it gave Congress direct taxing power

w.a: The Constitution let citizens vote directly for senators and the president.
w.why: false in 1787; legislatures chose senators and electors

cards.q: Identify the precedents set by Washington as president.
cards.a: Washington set precedents the Constitution did not spell out: he formed a cabinet of department heads (Jefferson at State, Hamilton at the Treasury, Knox at War, Randolph as attorney general) to advise him; accepted the plain title 'Mr. President'; took the lead in foreign policy with the 1793 neutrality proclamation; used federal force to uphold federal law in the Whiskey Rebellion; and stepped down after two terms, a custom kept until 1940.
cards.h: → four or five precedents, each specific
cards.n: Listing precedents without saying the Constitution did not require them misses why they matter: Washington turned a text into working institutions.

cards.q: Identify the Judiciary Act of 1789.
cards.a: The Judiciary Act of 1789 created the federal court system the Constitution only outlined: a Supreme Court of six justices, thirteen district courts and three circuit courts, plus the office of attorney general. Its Section 25 let the Supreme Court review state court decisions involving federal law, a key step in making national law supreme.
cards.h: → what it created + why it was needed
cards.n: An illustrative example. Confusing it with the Constitution is a slip: Article III left the lower courts and the Court's size to Congress, and this act filled them in.

cards.q: Identify the Whiskey Rebellion and give its year.
cards.a: In 1794 farmers in western Pennsylvania rose against the 1791 federal excise tax on whiskey, which fell hardest on grain farmers who distilled their crops to transport and sell them. Washington called up about 13,000 militiamen from four states and rode with them part of the way; the rebels scattered without a battle. It showed that the new government could enforce federal law.
cards.h: → year + who + grievance + federal response + meaning
cards.n: Treating it as a replay of Shays' Rebellion misses the contrast: this time the national government raised an army and enforced its own law.

cards.q: Identify the election of 1796 and the flaw in the electoral system it exposed.
cards.a: In 1796, the first contested presidential election, Federalist John Adams won 71 electoral votes to Democratic-Republican Thomas Jefferson's 68. Under the original rule that the runner-up became vice president, Jefferson took that office, so the president and vice president came from rival parties, a flaw the Twelfth Amendment (1804) corrected.
cards.h: → candidates + result + the flaw it exposed
cards.n: Saying Jefferson was Adams's running mate is wrong; there were no tickets in the Constitution, and the runner-up rule paired rivals.

cards.q: Identify the four main parts of Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Hamilton proposed (1) funding the national debt at full face value, (2) federal assumption of the states' war debts, (3) a Bank of the United States (chartered 1791) to hold federal money, lend and issue a sound currency, and (4) revenue from import tariffs and a new excise tax on whiskey (1791). Together they aimed to establish the nation's credit and tie wealthy creditors to the new government.
cards.h: → four parts + the shared aim
cards.n: Calling the tariff purely protective is a slip: Congress set it mainly for revenue and rejected most of Hamilton's Report on Manufactures.

cards.q: Differentiate the funding of the national debt from the assumption of state debts in Hamilton's financial plan.
cards.a: Funding meant paying the national government's Revolutionary debt at full face value, by exchanging old certificates for new interest-bearing bonds, to establish the nation's credit; it was controversial because speculators had bought many certificates cheaply from veterans. Assumption meant the federal government also taking over the states' war debts (up to 21.5 million dollars), a separate step that angered states that had already paid theirs.
cards.h: → each term defined + its own controversy
cards.n: Merging the two into one 'debt plan' misses their separate objections: funding rewarded speculators; assumption burdened states that had paid.

cards.q: Identify the Compromise of 1790 (the 'dinner table bargain').
cards.a: The Compromise of 1790 was a bargain that, by Jefferson's later account, was struck at a dinner he hosted in June 1790: Madison agreed to let federal assumption of state debts pass Congress, and in exchange the permanent national capital would be built on the Potomac River, in the South, with Philadelphia as the temporary capital for ten years.
cards.h: → who + what each side gave + what each got
cards.n: Treating it as the Bank bargain is a slip: it traded assumption, not the Bank, for the capital's location.

cards.q: Contrast loose and strict construction of the Constitution using the Bank debate.
cards.a: Hamilton argued for loose construction: the necessary and proper clause implies power to use any reasonable means toward an enumerated end, so a bank that helps collect taxes and borrow money is constitutional. Jefferson argued for strict construction: powers not delegated are reserved to the states, and 'necessary' means indispensable, so a merely convenient bank is unconstitutional. Washington accepted Hamilton's view and signed the bill in 1791.
cards.h: → Hamilton's reading vs. Jefferson's + the outcome
cards.n: Stating each position without tying it to the clause and the Bank lists instead of contrasting; the dispute was the meaning of 'necessary'.

cards.q: Identify Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) and its central argument.
cards.a: In his Report on Manufactures (December 1791), Hamilton argued that the government should actively promote manufacturing with protective tariffs, bounties (subsidies) and improved transportation, to diversify the economy, put more people to work and end dependence on British goods. Congress rejected most of it, but it became a blueprint for later protectionist policies.
cards.h: → date + proposals + purpose + fate
cards.n: Saying Congress adopted it is wrong; its subsidies were rejected in the 1790s, and its influence came later.

cards.q: Contrast Hamilton's and Jefferson's visions of the ideal American economy.
cards.a: Hamilton wanted a diversified commercial economy of trade, finance and manufacturing, built on national credit, a national bank and tariffs, with wealthy investors tied to the government's success. Jefferson wanted an agrarian republic of independent farmers, whose landownership he believed secured the virtue and independence a republic needed; he distrusted banks, public debt and cities as sources of corruption and dependence.
cards.h: → each man's economy + the reason behind it
cards.n: Saying Jefferson opposed all trade misreads him: he wanted farmers to export surpluses; he objected to finance, factory cities and dependence.

cards.q: Contrast Hamiltonian Federalists and Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans.
cards.a: Federalists wanted a strong national government, loose construction, Hamilton's credit and banking system, closer ties to Britain, and leadership by men of wealth and education; their base was New England and the commercial Northeast. Democratic-Republicans wanted limited federal power, strict construction, a farmers' republic, sympathy for revolutionary France, and more trust in ordinary white men; their base was the South and the West.
cards.h: → paired points: power, Constitution, economy, abroad, base
cards.n: A list of each party's traits is not a contrast; pair each point side by side and name the dividing issue.

cards.q: Identify the rival partisan newspapers of the 1790s.
cards.a: John Fenno's Gazette of the United States (from 1789) championed Hamilton and the Federalists, while Philip Freneau's National Gazette (from 1791), whose editor Jefferson had given a State Department clerkship, attacked Hamilton's program; Benjamin Franklin Bache's Philadelphia Aurora later took up the Republican cause. The papers spread party loyalties beyond Congress and made the opposition press a target of the Sedition Act.
cards.h: → each paper + its side + what the press war did
cards.n: An illustrative example. Calling these papers neutral reporting misses their purpose: each was a party organ that built partisan loyalty.

cards.q: Identify the Democratic-Republican societies of the 1790s.
cards.a: The Democratic-Republican societies were several dozen local political clubs formed from 1793, many inspired by the French Revolution and by the French envoy Edmond Genet's visit, that criticized Federalist policies such as Hamilton's finances, neutrality and Jay's Treaty. Washington blamed 'self-created societies' for encouraging the Whiskey Rebellion, and Federalists saw organized popular opposition as illegitimate.
cards.h: → what they were + when + what they opposed + reaction
cards.n: Treating them as the Democratic-Republican Party itself overstates them; they were local clubs that fed the opposition's growth.

cards.q: Identify the Proclamation of Neutrality of 1793.
cards.a: In April 1793, after revolutionary France and Britain went to war, Washington proclaimed that the United States would be impartial toward the warring powers, despite the 1778 alliance with France. It kept the weak nation out of a European war and asserted the president's lead in foreign policy, but Democratic-Republicans charged that it betrayed an ally and a sister republic.
cards.h: → date + context + what it declared + reaction
cards.n: Saying it ended the French alliance overstates it; the 1778 treaty stayed in force until 1800, and the proclamation did not mention it.

cards.q: Identify Jay's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: Jay's Treaty (signed 1794, approved by the Senate in 1795) with Britain secured British withdrawal from its forts in the Northwest by 1796 and sent prewar debts and boundary disputes to arbitration, but won nothing on impressment or neutral shipping rights. It averted war with Britain amid ship seizures, yet Democratic-Republicans denounced it, and the fight over it hardened the parties.
cards.h: → year + gains + failures + political effect
cards.n: Calling it a triumph or a pure surrender both miss the point: it bought peace and the forts at the price of neutral rights, and it split the parties.

cards.q: Identify Pinckney's Treaty and give its year.
cards.a: Pinckney's Treaty (the Treaty of San Lorenzo, 1795) with Spain gave Americans free navigation of the Mississippi River and the right of deposit at New Orleans to store goods for export, and set Spanish Florida's northern border at the 31st parallel. Spain, fearing a British-American alliance after Jay's Treaty, conceded what western farmers most needed.
cards.h: → year + terms + why Spain agreed
cards.n: Confusing it with Jay's Treaty is the classic slip: Jay dealt with Britain and the forts; Pinckney with Spain and the Mississippi.

cards.q: State the main advice of Washington's Farewell Address.
cards.a: In his Farewell Address (1796), Washington urged Americans to value national unity above loyalty to section, warned against the 'baneful effects of the spirit of party', and advised the nation to 'steer clear of permanent alliances' while trading with all nations. He also urged support for public credit, religion and morality.
cards.h: → unity + parties + alliances
cards.n: Saying Washington urged isolation from all foreign contact misreads it: he warned against permanent alliances while favoring commerce with every nation.

cards.q: Identify the historical situation and the purpose of Washington's Farewell Address (1796).
cards.a: Situation: Washington published it in September 1796 as he declined a third term, amid bitter party conflict over Hamilton's program and Jay's Treaty, while Britain and France were at war and French diplomats openly courted the Democratic-Republicans. Purpose: to urge Americans to put national unity above party and section and to avoid permanent alliances, a warning aimed at pro-French partisans as well as at future generations. Hamilton helped draft it.
cards.h: → situation (when, amid what) + purpose (aimed at whom)
cards.n: Treating it as timeless neutral advice ignores its situation; its warnings against faction and foreign influence had partisan targets in 1796.

cards.q: Identify the XYZ Affair.
cards.a: In 1797 French agents, named in published dispatches only as X, Y and Z, told three American envoys sent by President Adams that talks would require a bribe for Foreign Minister Talleyrand and a loan to France. Made public in 1798, the insult set off a wave of anti-French feeling, a Federalist surge, the undeclared Quasi-War at sea and the Alien and Sedition Acts.
cards.h: → year + what happened + consequences
cards.n: Treating the affair as a French declaration of war is wrong; it produced an undeclared naval war and a domestic crackdown on dissent.

cards.q: Identify the Quasi-War with France.
cards.a: The Quasi-War (1798-1800) was an undeclared naval war with France, which had been seizing American merchant ships after Jay's Treaty. Congress created a Navy Department, built warships and ended the 1778 treaties, and American ships fought French privateers in the Caribbean. Adams, defying his party's war faction, sent a new peace mission, and the Convention of 1800 ended the conflict and the alliance.
cards.h: → dates + cause + fighting + how it ended
cards.n: Calling it a declared war is wrong; Adams resisted Federalist pressure for full war, which split his party before the election of 1800.

cards.q: Identify the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
cards.a: The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798), passed by the Federalist Congress during the Quasi-War, were four laws: the Naturalization Act raised the residency requirement for citizenship from 5 to 14 years; the Alien Friends and Alien Enemies Acts let the president deport or detain dangerous foreigners; and the Sedition Act made it a crime to publish 'false, scandalous and malicious' writing against the government. It was used against Republican editors and Congressman Matthew Lyon.
cards.h: → year + context + the four laws + how they were used
cards.n: Treating them only as wartime security measures misses their partisan use: prosecutions fell almost entirely on Democratic-Republican critics.

cards.q: State what the Naturalization Act of 1798 changed and why the Federalists wanted it.
cards.a: The Naturalization Act of 1798 raised the residency requirement for U.S. citizenship from 5 to 14 years. Federalists wanted it because recent immigrants, especially Irish and French arrivals, tended to support the Democratic-Republicans, so a longer wait delayed their votes. Jefferson's Congress restored the five-year requirement in 1802.
cards.h: → the change + the partisan motive + its fate
cards.n: Treating it as a security law only misses its partisan aim: delaying citizenship delayed opposition votes.

cards.q: Identify the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions.
cards.a: The Kentucky (1798, 1799) and Virginia (1798) Resolutions, secretly written by Jefferson and Madison, declared the Alien and Sedition Acts unconstitutional. They argued that states could judge when Congress exceeded its powers; Virginia's called on states to 'interpose', and Kentucky's 1799 resolution named 'nullification' as the rightful remedy. No other state endorsed them, but they became a founding text of states' rights.
cards.h: → authors + year + what they claimed + response
cards.n: Saying they nullified the acts in practice overstates them: no other state joined, and most of the laws expired or were repealed by 1802.

cards.q: Define the compact theory of the Union laid out in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.
cards.a: The compact theory held that the states created the Constitution as a compact among themselves, so the federal government had only the powers the states had delegated, and each state could judge for itself when Congress exceeded them. Jefferson and Madison used it in 1798 to declare the Alien and Sedition Acts void; later defenders of nullification and secession built on it.
cards.h: → who made the Constitution + what states may do
cards.n: Taking the theory as settled law is a trap: Federalists answered that the people, not the states, made the Constitution, and the federal courts decide.

cards.q: Place these events of the 1790s in chronological order: Jay's Treaty, Whiskey Rebellion, Alien and Sedition Acts, Farewell Address, Pinckney's Treaty, XYZ Affair.
cards.a: Whiskey Rebellion (summer 1794) → Jay's Treaty (signed November 1794) → Pinckney's Treaty (1795) → Farewell Address (September 1796) → XYZ Affair (1797, made public 1798) → Alien and Sedition Acts (1798).
cards.h: → six events, earliest first, with years
cards.n: Placing the Alien and Sedition Acts before the XYZ Affair reverses cause and effect: the war scare after XYZ produced the acts.

cards.q: Identify the Spanish mission system in California and its effects.
cards.a: From San Diego in 1769, Franciscans led by Junipero Serra, backed by soldiers in presidios, built a chain of missions along the California coast (21 by 1823) to convert Native peoples and hold the region against Russian and British rivals. Missions ran on the bonded labor of converted Native people, who could not leave freely and died in large numbers of disease. Soldiers and settlers found chances to gain land and status, and Spanish, Catholic and Native cultures blended.
cards.h: → when + who + purpose + labor + social and cultural effects
cards.n: Describing the missions as purely religious misses the key concept's points: Native bonded labor, soldiers' social mobility and cultural blending.

cards.q: Explain why political parties emerged in the 1790s despite the Founders' hostility to them.
cards.a: Hamilton's program and the war between Britain and revolutionary France forced lasting choices about federal power, the economy and foreign policy. Each side came to see the other as a threat to the republic, so leaders built newspapers, clubs and voter networks, turning factions into parties.
cards.h: → Hamilton's program + French Revolution divide leaders → each sees a threat → press and voter networks → parties
cards.n: Naming the two parties is not a cause; the answer needs the specific disputes that divided leaders.
o: Regional economies pulled apart: commercial New England favored Hamilton's credit system, while southern and western farmers opposed it.
Jay's Treaty forced every member of Congress to take a side on Britain, hardening loose alignments into party voting.

w.a: Parties emerged because the Constitution required a two-party system.
w.why: false; the Constitution never mentions parties

w.a: Parties formed because Washington founded the Federalist Party to win the presidency.
w.why: wrong; Washington deplored parties and ran unopposed

cards.q: Explain why Virginia and other states without large war debts opposed Hamilton's assumption plan.
cards.a: Virginia and some other states had already paid off much of their war debt, so assumption would tax their citizens to pay debts owed mainly by states such as Massachusetts and South Carolina. Critics also saw it enriching speculators and strengthening federal power over the states.
cards.h: → Virginia had paid its debts → assumption taxes Virginians for others' debts + enriches speculators → opposition
cards.n: 'It was unfair' is a verdict, not an explanation; the point is who would pay whose debts, and the fear of federal and speculator power.
o: Critics feared that making creditors dependent on the federal treasury would build a moneyed interest loyal to Hamilton's government.
The dispute was settled only by the Compromise of 1790, which traded assumption for a southern capital on the Potomac.

w.a: Virginia opposed assumption because it wanted to keep paying its own large debts.
w.why: reversed; Virginia had already paid much of its debt

w.a: Virginia opposed assumption because it would move the capital to New York.
w.why: the deal put the capital on the Potomac

cards.q: Explain why the war between Britain and revolutionary France deepened party conflict in the United States.
cards.a: Federalists, tied to British trade and alarmed by the French Revolution's violence, leaned toward Britain; Democratic-Republicans saw France as a sister republic and resented British ship seizures. Each crisis, from neutrality to Jay's Treaty and the XYZ Affair, forced a choice that sharpened the divide.
cards.h: → Britain-France war → Federalists lean British, Republicans French → Jay, XYZ force choices → parties harden
cards.n: 'People disagreed about Europe' earns nothing; tie each party's position to interests or ideals and to a specific crisis.
o: Foreign policy became a test of loyalty, so each party accused the other of serving a foreign power, which Federalists used to justify the Sedition Act.
Seizures of American ships by both powers made neutral trading rights a practical economic issue for merchants and farmers.

w.a: The United States joined France's war against Britain in 1793.
w.why: false; Washington proclaimed neutrality

w.a: Both parties agreed on foreign policy and differed only over taxes.
w.why: ignores their split over Britain and France

cards.q: Explain why the uncertain legal relationship between the federal government and American Indian nations led to conflict over land in the 1790s.
cards.a: The federal government treated Native nations as sovereign enough to sign treaties, yet claimed ultimate power over their land, while settlers and states ignored treaty lines. Nations of the Ohio country resisted by war, and their defeat forced cessions such as the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.
cards.h: → nations are treaty partners, but U.S. claims their land → settlers ignore treaties → war → forced cessions
cards.n: Naming battles without the legal ambiguity, treaty partners whose land the U.S. claimed, misses the cause the key concept names.
o: The 1790 Intercourse Act required federal approval for buying Native land, but the government could not stop settlers or states from ignoring it.
Federal officials hoped to 'civilize' Native peoples through farming and assimilation, a policy that assumed their land would pass to settlers.

w.a: The federal government treated Native nations as foreign countries and never took their land.
w.why: false; treaties often forced cessions

w.a: The United States signed no treaties with Native nations in the 1790s.
w.why: false; Greenville and others were treaties

cards.q: Explain why the election of 1800 is called the 'Revolution of 1800.'
cards.a: For the first time, power passed from one party to its rival peacefully: defeated Federalists handed the presidency and Congress to Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans without violence. It showed the Constitution could survive partisanship, though a tie with Burr, broken by the House, led to the Twelfth Amendment.
cards.h: → bitter party contest → Federalists lose and step aside → first peaceful transfer → Constitution survives
cards.n: Describing the tie and the House vote without the peaceful transfer between rival parties misses why the name fits.
o: Jefferson himself called it a revolution in principle, a return to limited government and strict construction after Federalist rule.
The result ended Federalist control of the national government for good; the party never again won the presidency.

w.a: It was called a revolution because Jefferson took power by force.
w.why: false; the transfer was peaceful

w.a: It was a revolution because women and enslaved people gained the vote.
w.why: false; suffrage did not change

cards.q: Identify how painters of the Revolutionary era expressed a new national identity.
cards.a: Painters turned the Revolution and its leaders into shared national images. John Trumbull painted heroic Revolutionary scenes such as The Death of General Warren at the Battle of Bunker's Hill (1786) and The Declaration of Independence (begun 1786); Gilbert Stuart's 1796 portraits of Washington became the standard image of the first president; and Charles Willson Peale painted Revolutionary leaders and opened a Philadelphia museum of portraits and natural history (1786).
cards.h: → artist + work + what it made national
cards.n: Illustrative examples; the CED names no artists. Listing painters without saying how their work built a shared national story earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify how Noah Webster tried to create a distinctly American language and education.
cards.a: Noah Webster argued that 'as an independent nation, our honor requires us to have a system of our own, in language as well as government' (1789). His 'blue-backed' American Spelling Book (1783) taught generations of American children, and he promoted American spellings such as 'color' and 'center', later fixed in his American Dictionary (1828). He believed a common American speech and schooling would unite the states.
cards.h: → his aim + the speller + the spellings + why it mattered
cards.n: Illustrative example. Citing only the 1828 dictionary puts him in the wrong period; his Period 3 work was the 1783 speller and the call for an American standard.

cards.q: Identify how neoclassical architecture expressed the ideals of the new republic.
cards.a: Americans borrowed Greek and Roman forms, columns, domes and temple fronts, to link their republic with ancient self-government and Roman republican virtue. Jefferson modeled the Virginia State Capitol (designed 1785) on a Roman temple, the Maison Carree at Nimes, and Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan for Washington, D.C. set the Capitol and the President's House on a monumental scale fit for a new republic.
cards.h: → the style + the ideal it signaled + two examples
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Saying Americans copied British fashion misses the point: classical forms claimed the heritage of ancient republics, not of monarchy.

cards.q: Identify how writers of the Revolutionary era and early republic promoted a distinct American identity.
cards.a: Writers set out to show that the new nation had its own character. J. Hector St. John de Crevecoeur's Letters from an American Farmer (1782) asked 'What then is the American, this new man?' and described a people blended from many European nations; Royall Tyler's play The Contrast (1787) set a plain, honest American against a foppish imitator of British manners; and Mercy Otis Warren's satirical plays of the 1770s mocked royal officials.
cards.h: → writer + work + the idea of Americanness it offered
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Crevecoeur's 'new man' blended Europeans only; noting whom it left out, African and Native Americans, is what shows complexity.

cards.q: Identify two national symbols or rituals the United States created in its first decades.
cards.a: The Great Seal (adopted 1782), with its eagle and the motto 'E pluribus unum' ('out of many, one'), expressed a union made from many states. Fourth of July celebrations, held from 1777 with parades, toasts and readings of the Declaration, gave Americans a shared founding story. The cult of Washington, in portraits, birthday celebrations and nationwide mourning at his death in 1799, gave the nation a unifying hero.
cards.h: → two symbols or rituals + what each expressed
cards.n: Illustrative examples. Naming a symbol without what it expressed (unity of many states, a shared founding story) earns nothing.

cards.q: Identify regional differences that persisted alongside the new national culture in the 1790s.
cards.a: New England kept its town meetings, established Congregational churches and commercial, seafaring economy. The Middle States remained the most ethnically and religiously mixed, with Quakers, Germans and Scots-Irish. The South stayed rural and slaveholding, led by a planter gentry. The backcountry and trans-Appalachian West grew a frontier culture of small farms, evangelical religion and distrust of eastern elites. These regions shaped the parties' bases.
cards.h: → one trait per region + why it mattered
cards.n: Assuming national culture erased regional differences misses the key concept: it grew alongside them, and they resurfaced in party and sectional conflict.

cards.q: Explain why Americans after independence worked to create a national culture distinct from Britain's.
cards.a: Independence ended political ties but not cultural dependence: Americans still read British books and followed British tastes. Leaders believed a republic needed citizens loyal to something beyond their own states, so they promoted American schoolbooks, art, symbols and holidays to build a common identity.
cards.h: → political break but cultural dependence → republic needs shared loyalty → American books, art, symbols, holidays
cards.n: 'To be different from Britain' restates the question; name the dependence that remained and the civic need for unity.
o: The states shared little besides the Revolution, so celebrating its battles, heroes and Declaration became the common story that bound them.
European writers doubted that a republic could produce refined culture, and Americans set out to prove them wrong.

w.a: Americans built a national culture because Britain banned its books in the United States.
w.why: invented; British books kept circulating widely

w.a: By 1800 the new national culture had replaced all regional differences.
w.why: false; regional cultures persisted

cards.q: Explain why artists and architects of the early republic drew on classical Greek and Roman models.
cards.a: Americans saw their republic as the heir of ancient Athens and republican Rome, whose citizen virtue their political writers praised. Classical columns, temple fronts and heroic poses cast American leaders and buildings as embodiments of those republican ideals rather than of monarchy.
cards.h: → republic sees itself as heir of Athens and Rome → classical forms signal virtue and self-rule → buildings, art
cards.n: Describing columns and domes without the link to republican ideals shows no reasoning about identity.
o: An education steeped in Latin and ancient history made Roman figures natural models; Washington was praised as a modern Cincinnatus for giving up power.
Neoclassicism was fashionable across the Atlantic world in the 1780s, so Americans joined a wider style while giving it a republican meaning.

w.a: They used classical models because Greek and Roman builders designed the new Capitol.
w.why: anachronism; the architects were modern

w.a: Classical styles showed Americans' continuing loyalty to the British king.
w.why: reversed; they symbolized republics, not monarchy

cards.q: Explain why the national culture of the 1790s still carried strong continuities with colonial culture.
cards.a: Americans kept the English language, English common law, Protestant faith and many British tastes, and colonial regional patterns, New England towns, southern plantations and backcountry farms, persisted. The new national symbols and republican themes were layered on these older foundations rather than replacing them.
cards.h: → language, law, religion, tastes persist + colonial regions persist → new symbols layered on old foundations
cards.n: A continuity-and-change answer needs both sides; describing only the new symbols or only the continuities earns half at best.
o: Slavery and the exclusion of women from politics continued from colonial society, limiting whom the new culture treated as full Americans.
Even symbols of independence used familiar forms, such as sermons, printed pamphlets and toasts, to carry new republican meanings.

w.a: American culture broke completely with Britain after 1776.
w.why: overstated; language, law and religion continued

w.a: Americans stopped speaking English after independence to show their break with Britain.
w.why: false; Webster sought American spellings, not a new language

cards.q: Identify the Paxton Boys and their 1763 uprising.
cards.a: The Paxton Boys were Scots-Irish frontiersmen from around Paxton, Pennsylvania, who in December 1763, during Pontiac's War, murdered twenty peaceful Conestoga people, including those sheltered in the Lancaster workhouse. In early 1764 several hundred marched on Philadelphia to demand frontier defense and fairer representation; Benjamin Franklin persuaded them to turn back. It exposed the gulf between frontier settlers and an eastern, Quaker-influenced government.
cards.h: → who + when + what they did + what it revealed
cards.n: An illustrative example. Casting them as frontier defenders ignores that they killed peaceful Conestogas; the point is anti-Native violence and frontier-east tension.

cards.q: Identify the Regulator movement in the North and South Carolina backcountry.
cards.a: The Regulators were backcountry farmers in the Carolinas in the late 1760s and early 1770s. In South Carolina they policed outlaws and demanded courts for the backcountry; in North Carolina they protested corrupt local officials, heavy fees and taxes, and eastern control of the legislature, until Governor William Tryon's militia crushed them at the Battle of Alamance (1771). They show frontier anger at eastern elites.
cards.h: → where + when + grievances + outcome
cards.n: An illustrative example. Calling the Regulators Patriots fighting Britain is wrong; they fought their own colonial elites, and many later stayed neutral or Loyalist.

cards.q: Identify who moved west across the Appalachians in the 1780s and 1790s and the tensions their migration caused.
cards.a: Most migrants were farm families from the seaboard states, many of them Scots-Irish and German, along with enslaved people forced west by slaveholders moving to Kentucky and Tennessee; by 1800 several hundred thousand people lived west of the mountains. Their arrival brought war with Native nations, demands for use of the Mississippi, resentment of eastern taxes such as the whiskey excise, and talk in Kentucky of separate deals with Spain.
cards.h: → who moved + roughly how many + the tensions
cards.n: The population figure is an estimate. Treating the West as empty land misses the key concept: migration fueled ethnic, political and social tensions.

cards.q: Identify the first three new states admitted after the original thirteen.
cards.a: Vermont (1791), Kentucky (1792) and Tennessee (1796) were the first states admitted after the original thirteen. Kentucky and Tennessee, carved from Virginia's and North Carolina's western lands, show how fast migrants were crossing the Appalachians, and both entered as slave states, carrying slavery west.
cards.h: → three states in order + what they show
cards.n: Guessing Ohio is the trap: it came in 1803. The point is how quickly trans-Appalachian migration turned frontier into states.

cards.q: Identify St. Clair's Defeat of 1791 and the Native leaders who won it.
cards.a: In November 1791 the Western Confederacy, led by the Miami war leader Little Turtle and the Shawnee leader Blue Jacket, routed General Arthur St. Clair's army on the upper Wabash River, killing some 600 soldiers and many camp followers. It was the worst defeat the U.S. Army ever suffered against Native forces, and it forced Washington to build a larger, trained army under Anthony Wayne.
cards.h: → when + who won + scale + consequence
cards.n: Casualty figures are estimates. Assuming the United States easily outmatched Native nations misses how strong the Confederacy was until 1794.

cards.q: Identify the Battle of Fallen Timbers and the Treaty of Greenville.
cards.a: At Fallen Timbers (August 1794), near present-day Toledo, U.S. troops under General Anthony Wayne defeated the Western Confederacy of Shawnee, Miami, Delaware and other nations, whose British allies at nearby Fort Miamis then refused to shelter them. In the Treaty of Greenville (1795) the nations ceded most of present-day Ohio, opening it to rapid settlement.
cards.h: → battle: when, who + the treaty: what was ceded
cards.n: Leaving out the British refusal misses the key concept: Native nations weighed British alliances, and Jay's Treaty soon removed British forts from U.S. soil.

cards.q: Identify the effect of Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) on slavery.
cards.a: The cotton gin cleaned short-staple cotton quickly, so upland cotton could be grown profitably across the interior South. With British textile mills hungry for cotton, planters spread into the Georgia and South Carolina backcountry and toward new western lands, and slavery grew instead of fading as some revolutionaries had hoped; South Carolina even reopened its international slave trade in 1803.
cards.h: → what the machine did + the chain to slavery's growth
cards.n: Saying the gin reduced the need for enslaved labor reverses its effect: it removed a processing bottleneck, so demand for field labor grew.

cards.q: Contrast the Revolution's effects on slavery in the North and the South.
cards.a: In the North, revolutionary ideals and economies that did not depend on slave labor led every state from Pennsylvania north to begin abolition, mostly gradual, by 1804, and free Black communities built their own churches. In the South, the same ideals prompted some manumissions, especially in the Upper South, but slavery stayed central, and after the cotton gin it spread into the Deep South and the Southwest.
cards.h: → North: what and why + South: what and why
cards.n: Describing each region separately without naming the difference and its cause, economic dependence on slavery, lists rather than contrasts.

cards.q: Explain how the Revolution affected Native American peoples.
cards.a: Most Native nations sided with Britain to stop settler expansion, and they lost heavily: Patriot campaigns burned towns, as in Iroquois country in 1779, and the 1783 treaty gave their lands to the United States without consulting them. They then faced an expanding republic with no empire to play against it.
cards.h: → most side with Britain to stop settlers → towns burned, lands ceded without them → face U.S. expansion alone
cards.n: 'It was bad for them' earns nothing; name the alliance with Britain, the losses and the 1783 treaty's effect.
o: The war split nations internally, as with the Iroquois, whose Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Patriots.
Britain kept supplying Native allies from its posts after 1783, so Native resistance and Anglo-American tension continued into the 1790s.

w.a: The Revolution helped Native Americans because the new nation promised to protect their land.
w.why: false; the U.S. claimed their land under the 1783 treaty

w.a: Native nations stayed neutral and were untouched by the war.
w.why: false; most fought, and many were devastated

cards.q: Explain how the Iroquois Confederacy split during the American Revolution.
cards.a: The Confederacy's council could not reach its customary consensus, so each nation chose its own side: the Oneida and Tuscarora mostly backed the Patriots, while the Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga mostly joined Britain, some led by Joseph Brant. Iroquois fought Iroquois, as at Oriskany in 1777.
cards.h: → no consensus → each nation weighs ties, land → Oneida, Tuscarora with Patriots; four with Britain → civil war
cards.n: Listing the sides is only half; say why the tradition of unanimity broke and what the split cost the Confederacy.
o: Missionary ties drew many Oneida toward the colonists, while the Mohawk's long ties to the family of the British Indian agent William Johnson drew them to Britain.
After the war many pro-British Iroquois moved to Canada with Brant, while those who stayed lost most of their land in treaties with New York and the United States.

w.a: All six Iroquois nations fought for the Patriots in return for citizenship.
w.why: false; most fought for Britain

w.a: The Iroquois split because France asked some nations to fight for it.
w.why: France was not their ally in this war

cards.q: Explain why British alliances with American Indian nations increased tensions between the United States and Britain after 1783.
cards.a: Britain kept its forts on U.S. soil in the Northwest and supplied Native nations resisting American settlement, hoping to keep a buffer and the fur trade. Americans blamed British arms for Native victories such as St. Clair's defeat, so the forts became a grievance settled only by Jay's Treaty.
cards.h: → Britain keeps forts, arms Native allies → Native resistance → Americans blame Britain → Jay's Treaty
cards.n: Mentioning the forts without linking British supplies to Native resistance and American anger shows no causal chain.
o: Native nations judged the alliance by results: when the British refused to open Fort Miamis after Fallen Timbers, the Confederacy made peace at Greenville.
The pattern returned before the War of 1812, when Americans again blamed Britain for backing Tecumseh's confederacy.

w.a: Britain left North America entirely after the 1783 treaty.
w.why: false; it kept Canada and posts on U.S. soil

w.a: Native nations allied with Britain because it promised them U.S. citizenship.
w.why: invented; they sought help protecting their land

cards.q: Explain why attitudes toward slavery became more regional between 1754 and 1800.
cards.a: In 1754 slavery was legal in every colony and rarely questioned. Revolutionary ideals and a small economic stake led the North to begin abolition, while the South, whose wealth rested on enslaved labor, kept slavery, and the cotton gin after 1793 tied its future more tightly to it.
cards.h: → 1754 legal everywhere → ideals + small stake → northern abolition; southern dependence + cotton → entrenchment
cards.n: Describing northern abolition alone is half a continuity-and-change answer; show the 1754 baseline, the change and what stayed the same in the South.
o: The Northwest Ordinance's ban and the 1808 slave trade clause drew early political lines that later sectional conflicts built on.
The Upper South wavered, with rising manumissions in Virginia and Maryland, while the Deep South hardened, so the South itself was not uniform.

w.a: By 1800 every state except South Carolina had abolished slavery.
w.why: false; slavery stayed legal across the South

w.a: Attitudes did not change, because all Americans already opposed slavery in 1754.
w.why: false; slavery was legal and widely accepted

cards.q: Contrast the arguments colonists made in 1776 with those Anti-Federalists made in 1787.
cards.a: Similarity: both feared distant, unaccountable power, taxation by a government the people could not control, and standing armies, and both defended local self-government. Difference: in 1776 the threat was an outside power, Parliament and the Crown, and the answer was independence; in 1787 Anti-Federalists feared a national government Americans had designed themselves, and they sought amendments within the republic.
cards.h: → one similarity + one difference, each explained
cards.n: A contrast that names only differences misses the continuity; the strong answer shows the same fear aimed at a new target.

cards.q: Contrast the government's response to Shays' Rebellion and the Whiskey Rebellion.
cards.a: Under the Articles, Congress could raise no force against Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787), so Massachusetts relied on a militia paid for by private merchants. Under the Constitution, Washington called up about 13,000 militiamen from four states in 1794 and marched them against the Whiskey rebels to enforce a federal tax. The contrast shows the shift from a Congress that could only request to a government that could act.
cards.h: → 1786 response + 1794 response + what changed
cards.n: Describing the two rebellions without naming the change in federal power between them misses the point of the pairing.

cards.q: Identify one continuity and one change in the relationship between Americans and a central authority from 1754 to 1800.
cards.a: Continuity: Americans kept resisting distant central power, from colonial assemblies rejecting the Albany Plan (1754) and colonists resisting Parliament's taxes, to the Anti-Federalists' fight against ratification and the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798). Change: the central authority itself changed, from Parliament and the Crown, to a weak Confederation Congress (1781), to a national government under the Constitution (1789) that could tax and enforce its laws.
cards.h: → a continuity with evidence + a change with evidence
cards.n: Naming a change without the continuity, or the reverse, answers half; each needs specific evidence from across the period.

cards.q: Describe a broader historical context for an essay on the debate over ratifying the Constitution (1787-1788).
cards.a: Since independence, Americans had built governments meant to prevent tyranny: state constitutions with powerful legislatures and weak governors, and the Articles of Confederation, whose Congress could not tax, regulate trade or enforce laws. By 1786 unpaid war debts, trade troubles with Britain and Spain, and Shays' Rebellion convinced many leaders that the Confederation was failing, while others still feared the concentrated power they had fought Britain to escape.
cards.h: → earlier experiments + the crisis that led to 1787
cards.n: Using Federalist No. 10 or the Bill of Rights as 'context' earns nothing; those are evidence for the argument, not the broader setting before it.

cards.q: Write a thesis for this prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the American Revolution changed American society from 1775 to 1800.
cards.a: The Revolution changed American politics more than American society: it replaced monarchy with republican governments based on consent and gave more white men a political voice, but it left slavery entrenched in the South, women without political rights, and property qualifications in place, so its social changes, such as northern gradual emancipation and republican motherhood, were real but limited.
cards.h: → claim of extent + categories that set the reasoning
cards.n: Restating the prompt ('it changed society to a great extent') earns nothing; the thesis must take a position and name the categories the essay will argue.

cards.q: Support the claim that competition for land and trade in North America produced conflict throughout 1754-1800, using three pieces of evidence from different decades.
cards.a: 1750s: British colonists' push into the Ohio valley, claimed by France and its Native allies, started the French and Indian War in 1754. 1760s: Pontiac's Rebellion (1763) against British rule and advancing settlers led to the Proclamation line, which colonists resented. 1790s: the war for the Ohio country, from St. Clair's defeat (1791) to Fallen Timbers (1794), and disputes with Britain over forts and Spain over the Mississippi, settled by Jay's and Pinckney's Treaties.
cards.h: → one piece per decade, each tied to the claim
cards.n: Three events from one decade prove no continuity; the evidence must span the period, and each piece must be tied back to the claim.

cards.q: Explain the limits of the American Revolution as a social revolution.
cards.a: The Revolution overturned monarchy, abolished titles, ended the Anglican establishment in the South and widened white men's voice, but it left slavery entrenched in the South, women without political rights, property qualifications in place and Native nations losing land. Its social change was real but narrow.
cards.h: → monarchy, titles, establishment gone + wider white male voice → slavery, women, property rules, Native losses remain
cards.n: Listing only the limits, or only the changes, earns less; the verb asks for limits measured against the real changes.
o: Historians such as Gordon Wood argue the Revolution was radical in changing how Americans thought about hierarchy and deference, even where laws stayed the same.
The Revolution's own language later fueled the abolition and women's rights movements, so its limits in 1800 were not permanent.

w.a: The Revolution freed all enslaved people and gave women the vote.
w.why: false; neither happened

w.a: Nothing in American society changed because of the Revolution.
w.why: ignores disestablishment, northern emancipation and wider suffrage

cards.q: Explain why the United States' relationship with European powers changed between 1754 and 1800.
cards.a: In 1754 the colonies were part of Britain's empire, fighting France. Independence, won with French help, made the United States a weak nation among rival empires, so by the 1790s it sought safety in neutrality, treaties with Britain and Spain, and Washington's warning against permanent alliances.
cards.h: → colonies inside Britain's empire → French alliance wins independence → weak new nation → neutrality, treaties
cards.n: Naming treaties without the shift from colony to independent neutral misses the change the question asks for.
o: Continuity: throughout the period Americans needed secure western borders and access to the Mississippi, whether as British colonists or as U.S. citizens.
By 1798 the former ally France had become the enemy in the Quasi-War, showing how quickly alignments shifted once the nation pursued its own interests.

w.a: The United States stayed allied with France through the 1790s and fought Britain.
w.why: false; it proclaimed neutrality and fought France at sea

w.a: European powers left North America entirely after 1783.
w.why: false; Britain and Spain kept territories and forts

cards.q: Explain why the independence movement drew ordinary colonists into politics between 1765 and 1800.
cards.a: Resistance depended on mass action: boycotts, crowd protests, committees and militias involved artisans, laborers and women. Having acted politically, ordinary men expected a voice, so states widened representation, and in the 1790s the parties courted voters through newspapers and clubs.
cards.h: → resistance needs boycotts, crowds, militias → ordinary people act → expect a voice → wider politics, party mobilizing
cards.n: Describing protests without their effect on who took part in politics afterward misses the change over time.
o: Revolutionary language of consent and equality gave excluded groups, such as women and free Black Americans, words to press their claims, even when they were refused.
The war was fought largely by militias and a citizen army, which made service a basis for demanding political rights.

w.a: Ordinary colonists stayed out of politics because only the Founders took part in the Revolution.
w.why: false; artisans, laborers and women were central to resistance

w.a: Every adult American gained the vote after 1776.
w.why: false; property, sex and race still excluded many

cards.q: Define Jeffersonian democracy as a governing philosophy.
cards.a: Jefferson's vision of a limited federal government, strict construction of the Constitution, low taxes and debt, reduced military, and a republic anchored in independent yeoman farmers rather than merchants and financiers.
cards.h: → two-part: size of government + social base
cards.n: Watch the gap between theory and practice: Jefferson the strict constructionist bought Louisiana and kept the Bank running.

cards.q: Date the Revolution of 1800 and the constitutional fix it produced.
cards.a: Election of 1800; the Jefferson-Burr tie in the Electoral College was resolved by the House in 1801, and the 12th Amendment (1804) required separate ballots for president and vice president.
cards.h: → year + amendment
cards.n: The tie was between two Republicans, not between parties; Hamilton's lobbying for Jefferson over Burr led toward their 1804 duel.

cards.q: Identify the Louisiana Purchase and its terms.
cards.a: The 1803 purchase of roughly 828,000 square miles from France for about $15 million, doubling the size of the United States and giving the U.S. control of New Orleans and the Mississippi River outlet.
cards.h: → who sold, what it doubled
cards.n: Napoleon sold after the Haitian Revolution wrecked his plans for a New World empire.

cards.q: Date the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition.
cards.a: Louisiana Purchase 1803; the Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery expedition ran 1804-1806.
cards.h: → two dates, purchase then exploration
cards.n: Jefferson the strict constructionist found no express power to buy land, so this is the standard example of principle yielding to opportunity.

cards.q: Explain the constitutional dilemma the Louisiana Purchase created for Jefferson.
cards.a: Jefferson was a strict constructionist, but the Constitution nowhere authorized buying territory. He accepted a loose-construction reading of the treaty power to close the deal, contradicting his own principles.
cards.h: → strict vs loose construction
cards.n: A favorite irony question: the strict constructionist used implied powers when it served national interest.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Marbury v. Madison (1803).
cards.a: The Marshall Court held that Marbury was legally entitled to his commission, but that it could not order its delivery: the section of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that gave the Court original jurisdiction to issue such writs of mandamus conflicted with Article III and was unconstitutional. This established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review over acts of Congress.
cards.h: → what power the Court claimed
cards.n: The Court gained power by declining a power; that paradox is the standard exam point.

cards.q: Define judicial review.
cards.a: The power of the federal courts to declare acts of Congress, the executive, or the states unconstitutional and therefore void. It is not written in the Constitution; it was asserted by the Court in Marbury v. Madison.
cards.h: → power to strike down what
cards.n: Marbury (1803) voided part of the Judiciary Act of 1789; the Court struck down no other federal law until Dred Scott in 1857.

cards.q: Identify the holding of McCulloch v. Maryland (1819).
cards.a: Congress could charter the Bank of the United States under the necessary and proper clause (implied powers), and Maryland could not tax it because the power to tax involves the power to destroy. Federal law is supreme over state law.
cards.h: → implied powers + no state tax
cards.n: The strongest single case for expanded federal power in Period 4.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).
cards.a: The Court struck down a New York steamboat monopoly, holding that Congress alone regulates interstate commerce and defining commerce broadly to include navigation. State laws conflicting with federal commerce regulation are void.
cards.h: → which clause, which level of government
cards.n: The commerce clause reading here is the foundation for later federal economic regulation.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Fletcher v. Peck (1810).
cards.a: The Court voided a Georgia law rescinding a corrupt Yazoo land grant, ruling that the grant was a contract protected by the Constitution. It was the first time the Court struck down a state law as unconstitutional.
cards.h: → contract clause, first of its kind
cards.n: Pair with Dartmouth: both protect contracts and property against state legislatures.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819).
cards.a: New Hampshire could not alter Dartmouth's colonial charter because a charter is a contract protected by the contract clause. The ruling shielded private corporations from state interference and encouraged corporate growth.
cards.h: → charter as contract
cards.n: Useful evidence that the Marshall Court favored a national business climate over state control.

cards.q: Identify the holding of Worcester v. Georgia (1832) and what followed.
cards.a: The Court ruled the Cherokee Nation a distinct political community over which Georgia law had no force, so removal was illegal. Jackson declined to enforce the decision and removal proceeded anyway.
cards.h: → ruling + non-enforcement
cards.n: The classic example of the judiciary lacking enforcement power; do not confuse it with Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831).

cards.q: Explain the overall direction of the Marshall Court's decisions.
cards.a: The Court consistently strengthened the federal government against the states, protected contracts and property rights, and expanded the reach of the commerce clause, building a national legal framework for a market economy.
cards.h: → one trend in three areas
cards.n: Marshall was a Federalist appointee whose rulings outlasted the Federalist Party itself.

cards.q: Define the Embargo Act of 1807 and state its purpose.
cards.a: A law banning nearly all American exports to foreign ports, intended to force Britain and France to respect U.S. neutral shipping rights and stop impressment by depriving them of American goods.
cards.h: → what was banned, to pressure whom
cards.n: It wrecked New England shipping far more than Britain's trade, bred smuggling, and was replaced in 1809 by the Non-Intercourse Act.

cards.q: Explain why the Embargo Act backfired.
cards.a: Britain found other suppliers while the American economy, especially New England shipping, collapsed. Smuggling spread, Federalist opposition revived, and the embargo was repealed in 1809 without changing British policy.
cards.h: → who was hurt most
cards.n: It ironically spurred domestic manufacturing, which supports arguments about the roots of the Market Revolution.

cards.q: Explain the causes of the War of 1812.
cards.a: British impressment of American sailors and seizure of neutral shipping, British support for Native resistance in the Northwest led by Tecumseh, and pressure from western and southern War Hawks such as Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun who wanted Canada and Florida.
cards.h: → three causes: sea, frontier, politics
cards.n: New England opposed the war it was supposedly fought to protect, a favorite contradiction on the exam.

cards.q: State the consequences of the War of 1812.
cards.a: Territorial boundaries were unchanged by the Treaty of Ghent, but American nationalism surged, the Federalist Party collapsed, domestic manufacturing grew, Native resistance east of the Mississippi was broken, and Andrew Jackson became a national hero after New Orleans.
cards.h: → list of five outcomes
cards.n: Called the Second War of Independence even though militarily it was roughly a draw.

cards.q: Date the War of 1812, the Treaty of Ghent, and the Battle of New Orleans.
cards.a: War declared June 1812; Treaty of Ghent signed December 1814; Battle of New Orleans fought January 1815, after the treaty was signed but before news reached America.
cards.h: → three dates in order
cards.n: The out-of-order sequence (treaty before the famous victory) is a common trap.

cards.q: Identify the Hartford Convention.
cards.a: An 1814-1815 meeting of New England Federalists who protested the War of 1812, proposed constitutional amendments limiting southern and western power, and discussed secession or a separate peace.
cards.h: → who met, what they demanded
cards.n: It met just as news of New Orleans and peace arrived, making the delegates look disloyal.

cards.q: Explain how the Hartford Convention destroyed the Federalist Party.
cards.a: Its complaints and secession talk arrived at the exact moment of Jackson's victory at New Orleans and the peace treaty, so Federalists appeared unpatriotic and even treasonous. The party never won a national election again.
cards.h: → timing, then reputation
cards.n: Ironically Federalists used states-rights and nullification arguments they had long opposed.

cards.q: Define the Era of Good Feelings.
cards.a: The period roughly 1815-1825 under Monroe when the Federalist Party had collapsed and one-party rule created an appearance of political harmony, alongside surging nationalism after the War of 1812.
cards.h: → years + why it looked harmonious
cards.n: The name is misleading: the Panic of 1819 and the Missouri crisis show deep sectional and economic conflict.

cards.q: Define Henry Clay's American System.
cards.a: A three-part nationalist economic program: a protective tariff to shield American manufacturing, a national bank to provide stable currency and credit, and federally funded internal improvements such as roads and canals.
cards.h: → three parts
cards.n: Southerners resisted the tariff and federally funded improvements, so it was only partly enacted.

cards.q: Identify the terms of the Missouri Compromise.
cards.a: Missouri entered as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the Senate balanced, and slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes.
cards.h: → two states + a line
cards.n: The 36 30 line was later voided by Kansas-Nebraska (1854) and declared unconstitutional in Dred Scott (1857).

cards.q: Date the Missouri Compromise and the Panic that preceded it.
cards.a: Panic of 1819; Missouri Compromise 1820.
cards.h: → two consecutive years
cards.n: Jefferson called the Missouri crisis a fire bell in the night; the 36 30 line it drew is exactly what Kansas-Nebraska repealed in 1854.

cards.q: Explain why Jefferson called the Missouri crisis a fire bell in the night.
cards.a: The debate exposed slavery as a permanent sectional dividing line that could break the Union. Jefferson saw that drawing a geographic line over slavery would define politics for generations rather than settle the question.
cards.h: → what the crisis revealed
cards.n: Strong evidence for causation prompts tracing the long road to secession.

cards.q: State the Monroe Doctrine.
cards.a: Declared in 1823 that the Western Hemisphere was closed to further European colonization, that the U.S. would treat European intervention in the Americas as hostile, and that the U.S. would stay out of European affairs.
cards.h: → two rules, one for each hemisphere
cards.n: Britain's navy actually enforced it; the U.S. lacked the power to back it up in 1823.

cards.q: Date the Monroe Doctrine and the Adams-Onis Treaty.
cards.a: Adams-Onis Treaty (Florida ceded by Spain) 1819; Monroe Doctrine 1823.
cards.h: → treaty first, doctrine second
cards.n: Britain proposed a joint declaration; Adams insisted the United States speak alone, though the Royal Navy did the actual enforcing.

cards.q: Define the Market Revolution.
cards.a: The early 1800s shift from local subsistence and barter economies to interconnected regional markets, driven by new transportation, factory production, wage labor, and cash crops grown for distant sale.
cards.h: → from what economy to what economy
cards.n: It made the North and West economically interdependent while the South specialized in cotton, deepening sectionalism.

cards.q: Identify the Erie Canal and its economic effect.
cards.a: Completed in 1825, the state-funded canal linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie, slashed shipping costs between the Midwest and New York City, made New York the nation's leading port, and triggered a canal-building boom.
cards.h: → what it linked, which city won
cards.n: It swung western produce away from New Orleans and the Mississippi, tying the Old Northwest to the Northeast rather than to the South.

cards.q: Explain how the transportation revolution reshaped sectional alignments.
cards.a: Canals and then railroads ran east-west, tying western farms to northeastern cities and markets instead of shipping goods down the Mississippi to New Orleans. This bound the North and West together and left the South comparatively isolated.
cards.h: → direction of trade routes
cards.n: A strong causation point for why the West sided with the Union in 1861.

cards.q: Define the Lowell system.
cards.a: A Massachusetts textile model that recruited young unmarried farm women to live in supervised company boardinghouses and work in mechanized mills that combined spinning and weaving under one roof.
cards.h: → who worked, where they lived
cards.n: Lowell women organized some of the earliest labor protests in the U.S., including the 1834 and 1836 turnouts.

cards.q: Contrast the early Lowell workforce with the mill workforce by the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Early mills relied on native-born farm daughters working temporarily under paternalistic supervision. By the 1840s falling wages and speedups drove them out, and Irish immigrant families, including men and children, took the jobs at lower pay.
cards.h: → who was replaced by whom
cards.n: Good continuity-and-change evidence on the degradation of factory labor.

cards.q: Contrast Irish and German immigration in the 1840s-1850s.
cards.a: Irish, driven by the potato famine after 1845, who were mostly poor, Catholic, and settled in northeastern cities as laborers and domestic servants; and Germans, fleeing the failed revolutions of 1848 and land pressure, who often had some capital and moved to midwestern farms and cities.
cards.h: → two groups, push factor, destination
cards.n: The class difference explains why anti-Irish hostility was sharper than anti-German hostility.

cards.q: Define nativism and name its main political expression in the 1850s.
cards.a: Hostility toward immigrants and preference for native-born Protestants, driven by fear of Catholic influence and wage competition. Its political vehicle was the American Party, or Know-Nothings, which demanded longer naturalization periods and bans on immigrant officeholding.
cards.h: → definition + party name
cards.n: Nativism recurs in Period 6 and Period 7; use it for continuity-across-time prompts.

cards.q: Explain how the cotton gin expanded slavery.
cards.a: Whitney's 1793 gin made short-staple cotton profitable across the Deep South by mechanizing seed removal. Planters spread cotton cultivation west into Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas, and demand for enslaved field labor rose sharply.
cards.h: → invention, then geography, then labor
cards.n: The domestic slave trade moved roughly a million people from the Upper to the Deep South after 1808.

cards.q: Differentiate the international slave trade from the domestic slave trade after 1808.
cards.a: Congress banned importing enslaved people from abroad in 1808. The domestic trade then supplied Deep South cotton lands by selling roughly one million people from the Upper South southwest, breaking apart families within the United States rather than across the Atlantic.
cards.h: → external ban vs internal growth
cards.n: A key MIG theme item: the largest forced internal migration in U.S. history.

cards.q: Define the Second Great Awakening.
cards.a: A wave of Protestant revivalism from the 1790s through the 1830s that emphasized emotional conversion, free will, and the idea that individuals could achieve salvation and perfect society. Charles Grandison Finney was its leading preacher.
cards.h: → theology + leading preacher
cards.n: The doctrine of human perfectibility is the direct engine of antebellum reform.

cards.q: Explain the link between the Second Great Awakening and antebellum reform movements.
cards.a: Revivalists taught that people freely chose salvation and could perfect themselves and society, so believers, especially women, turned religious enthusiasm into organized campaigns against alcohol, slavery, illiteracy, and mistreatment of prisoners and the mentally ill.
cards.h: → doctrine, then organized action
cards.n: The single most reliable causation link in Period 4.

cards.q: Contrast the moral and the economic arguments for temperance.
cards.a: Moral reformers, drawing on the Second Great Awakening and led by groups such as the American Temperance Society founded in 1826, blamed drink for sin, poverty, and domestic violence. Employers backed temperance for practical reasons: sober workers meant fewer accidents and steadier factory output.
cards.h: → two motives, two constituencies
cards.n: Nativists tied drinking to Irish and German immigrants, entangling temperance with anti-immigrant politics.

cards.q: Identify William Lloyd Garrison and The Liberator.
cards.a: Garrison began publishing The Liberator in 1831, demanding immediate and uncompensated emancipation with no colonization, condemning the Constitution as a proslavery document, and founding the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833.
cards.h: → newspaper + immediatist demand
cards.n: Immediatism marked a sharp break from earlier gradual emancipation and colonization schemes.

cards.q: Identify Frederick Douglass and his contribution to abolition.
cards.a: An escaped enslaved man who became the movement's most powerful speaker, published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass in 1845, and founded the North Star in 1847, arguing that the Constitution could be used as an antislavery weapon.
cards.h: → narrative + newspaper + constitutional stance
cards.n: His split with Garrison over the Constitution and political action is a classic comparison question.

cards.q: Identify David Walker's Appeal.
cards.a: Walker's Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (1829) was a militant pamphlet by a free Black Bostonian that condemned slavery and racism and urged enslaved people to resist, by violence if necessary.
cards.h: → pamphlet, militant call
cards.n: Southern states banned it and blamed such writings for Nat Turner's 1831 rebellion.

cards.q: Contrast Garrison's and Douglass's strategies for ending slavery.
cards.a: Garrison rejected politics, burned the Constitution as a covenant with death, and urged moral suasion and northern disunion. Douglass came to argue that the Constitution was antislavery and that abolitionists should vote, organize parties, and use government power.
cards.h: → attitude toward the Constitution and voting
cards.n: Both are immediatists; the difference is means, not goals.

cards.q: Identify the Seneca Falls Convention.
cards.a: The first women's rights convention in the United States, held in New York in 1848 and organized by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott. It issued the Declaration of Sentiments demanding legal equality and, most controversially, suffrage.
cards.h: → who organized, what document
cards.n: Many attendees came out of abolitionism, where women were barred from speaking.

cards.q: State what the Declaration of Sentiments argued and what document it imitated.
cards.a: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence, it declared that all men and women are created equal and listed the injuries of men toward women, including denial of the vote, property rights, education, and legal standing in marriage.
cards.h: → model text + list of grievances
cards.n: Using the Declaration's form was a deliberate rhetorical claim to the Revolution's legacy.

cards.q: Date the Seneca Falls Convention and the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society and its female auxiliaries.
cards.a: American Anti-Slavery Society founded 1833 with women organizing female auxiliaries from 1833-1837; Seneca Falls Convention 1848.
cards.h: → abolition first, then Seneca Falls
cards.n: The exam wants the causal link: exclusion from abolitionist podiums, especially at London in 1840, is what pushed women to organize separately.

cards.q: Identify Dorothea Dix and her reform campaign.
cards.a: A Massachusetts teacher who documented the confinement of the mentally ill in jails and almshouses and lobbied state legislatures from the 1840s to build publicly funded asylums offering treatment rather than punishment.
cards.h: → population served + institution built
cards.n: Part of a broader shift toward state-run institutions, including penitentiaries designed to reform rather than merely punish.

cards.q: Identify Horace Mann and the common school movement.
cards.a: As Massachusetts secretary of education from 1837, Mann pushed for tax-supported public elementary schools, longer school years, standardized curricula, and teacher training in normal schools, arguing that education would make citizens and equalize opportunity.
cards.h: → what kind of school, funded how
cards.n: Teaching became a leading paid profession for women, which reformers justified as an extension of motherhood.

cards.q: Define utopian communities and name several examples.
cards.a: Experimental settlements that withdrew from mainstream society to model a perfected social order. Examples: the Shakers (celibacy and communal property), New Harmony (Owen's secular socialism), Oneida (complex marriage and communal child rearing), and Brook Farm (transcendentalist).
cards.h: → definition + named communities
cards.n: Most grew out of Second Great Awakening perfectionism, though Owen's New Harmony was secular; nearly all collapsed within a generation.

cards.q: Define transcendentalism.
cards.a: A New England intellectual movement led by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau holding that truth comes from intuition and nature rather than from institutions or empirical reason, and celebrating self-reliance and individual conscience.
cards.h: → source of truth + two figures
cards.n: Thoreau's Civil Disobedience, written against the Mexican-American War, later influenced Gandhi and King.

cards.q: Define the cult of domesticity.
cards.a: The middle-class ideal that emerged with the Market Revolution assigning women a separate private sphere of home, piety, purity, and child rearing, while men occupied the public world of work and politics.
cards.h: → separate spheres ideology
cards.n: It applied mainly to white middle-class women; poor, immigrant, and enslaved women worked outside the home.

cards.q: Contrast the cult of domesticity with the women's rights movement of the 1840s.
cards.a: The cult of domesticity confined women to a moral private sphere; the women's rights movement demanded entry to the public sphere through suffrage, property rights, and legal standing. Yet reformers often used domesticity's claim of female moral superiority to justify public activism.
cards.h: → opposed goals, shared premise
cards.n: The best answers note that domesticity both limited women and gave them a platform.

cards.q: Define Jacksonian democracy.
cards.a: The 1820s-1830s expansion of political participation through near-universal white male suffrage, popular election of presidential electors, nominating conventions, and rhetoric pitting the common man against entrenched elites and monopolies.
cards.h: → who gained the vote, who was excluded
cards.n: Expansion for white men coincided with the disfranchisement of free Black men in states like Pennsylvania and New York.

cards.q: Define the spoils system.
